a124.speaker: National Vision 2050 (Tanzania development vision document)
a124.name: National Vision 2050 (Tanzania development vision document)
a124.speech: Emphasises that lasting growth depends less on ambition or politics and more on the effectiveness of the systems supporting policies, institutions and national aspirations ; underlines that the country’s progress will be defined not just by plans on paper, but by the tangible impacts experienced by citizens in their daily lives.

a124.speaker: World Bank’s Independent Evaluation Group
a124.name: World Bank’s Independent Evaluation Group
a124.speech: Has long pinpointed high failure rates in infrastructure projects across Sub-Saharan Africa, often exceeding 50 per cent.

a127.speaker: International Monetary Fund (World Economic Outlook report)
a127.name: International Monetary Fund (World Economic Outlook report)
a127.speech: Slashed growth forecasts for most countries but stopped short of predicting a global recession, saying, “Our new growth projections will include notable markdowns, but not recession.” ; warned that global share prices have dropped “as trade tensions flared” and that there will be an “erosion of trust” among countries.

a127.speaker: IMF Fiscal Monitor report
a127.name: IMF Fiscal Monitor report
a127.speech: Warned of escalating uncertainty and policy shifts reshaping the fiscal outlook. “Global public debt projections have been revised upwards, while tariffs, uncertainty and market volatility, increased defence spending, and challenging foreign aid are intensifying risks” ; “Countries must implement gradual fiscal adjustments within credible medium-term frameworks to reduce debt and build buffers against heightened uncertainty. Reforms to major expenditure programs, such as energy subsidies and pensions, are crucial to reducing fiscal vulnerabilities while fostering growth.”

a127.speaker: IMF Global Financial Stability Report
a127.name: IMF Global Financial Stability Report
a127.speech: Warned that global financial stability risks have increased significantly, identifying three key forward-looking vulnerabilities: (i) valuations remain high in some key markets; (ii) some highly leveraged financial institutions and their nexus with banking systems; and (iii) risks of market turmoil and challenges to debt sustainability for highly indebted sovereigns; it ultimately warned that “major geopolitical risk events can trigger a significant decline in stock prices and raise sovereign risk premiums, thereby posing a potential threat to macro-financial stability.”

a127.speaker: IMF regional outlook report for sub-Saharan Africa
a127.name: IMF regional outlook report for sub-Saharan Africa
a127.speech: Said the hard-won recovery in sub-Saharan Africa has been overtaken by recent events: “The sudden shift in the global outlook has clouded the region’s short-term prospects and made policy even more challenging.”

a127.speaker: Ajay Banga, World Bank President
a127.name: Ajay Banga
a127.title: World Bank President
a127.speech: Told developing countries to strike swift trade deals with the United States at the “earliest possible” opportunity. “You need to negotiate trade systems with the US at the earliest possible (opportunity)”, he told AFP. “If you delay, it hurts everyone.”

a127.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva, Director-General of the International Monetary Fund
a127.name: Kristalina Georgieva
a127.title: Director-General of the International Monetary Fund
a127.speech: In a separate interview with reporters during the week, noted that member countries were anxious about the shock to a global economy buffeted by pandemic, inflation and wars but held out hope that trade negotiations would ease the tariff tensions. “We recognise that there is work underway to resolve trade disputes and reduce uncertainty. Uncertainty is really bad for business, so the sooner there is this cloud that is hanging over our heads is lifted, the better for profit, for growth, for the world economy.”

a127.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva, Director-General of the International Monetary Fund
a127.name: Kristalina Georgieva
a127.title: Director-General of the International Monetary Fund
a127.speech: At the press briefing on the global policy agenda: “Finally, we will reiterate the need for continued cooperation in a multipolar world. The shared objective for all must be a better balanced and more resilient world economy.”

a127.speaker: United States (notice of withdrawal from the World Health Organisation)
a127.name: United States (notice of withdrawal from the World Health Organisation)
a127.speech: Said it expressed the same sentiment in 2020 due to the organisation’s alleged “mishandling of the COVID-19 pandemic that arose out of Wuhan, China, and other global health crises, its failure to adopt urgently needed reforms, and its inability to demonstrate independence from the inappropriate political influence of WHO member states.”

a127.speaker: Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, Director-General of the World Trade Organisation
a127.name: Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala
a127.title: Director-General of the World Trade Organisation
a127.speech: Had noted that the WTO’s initial estimates suggested that the measures, “coupled with those introduced since the beginning of the year, could lead to an overall contraction of around 1% in global merchandise trade volumes this year, representing a downward revision of nearly four percentage points from previous projections.”

a127.speaker: Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, Director-General of the World Trade Organisation
a127.name: Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala
a127.title: Director-General of the World Trade Organisation
a127.speech: Speaking to Nigerian journalists on Friday, appealed to the US to take into account the effects of its tariff policies on least-developed countries, calling for review and negotiations.

a127.speaker: Reuters
a127.name: Reuters
a127.speech: Reported during the week that many finance and trade ministers sought to meet with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other key Trump administration officials, to no avail, adding that not a single deal was finalised over the course of the week despite the Trump administration touting negotiations and proposals.

a127.speaker: Andrzej Domanski, Polish Finance Minister
a127.name: Andrzej Domanski
a127.title: Polish Finance Minister
a127.speech: Told the medium that there was no negotiation but mere “discussions” during the week. “…(T)his uncertainty is bad for Europe, for the U.S. I mean, it’s actually bad for everyone.”

a127.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a127.name: Donald Trump
a127.title: US President
a127.speech: Has repeatedly denied the Project 2025 proposal for the US to pull out of the IMF and World Bank ; recently said he is unlikely to grant another 90-day pause on the tariffs but expects to be able to strike trade deals with a range of countries.

a169.speaker: Vera Songwe, Executive Secretary of the UN Economic Commission for Africa (ECA)
a169.name: Vera Songwe
a169.title: Executive Secretary of the UN Economic Commission for Africa (ECA)
a169.speech: Said that combatting bribery, money laundering and tax evasion should be a priority if Africa has to finance its transition to middle income status and increase prosperity. ; Called on governments to take action on several fronts, insisting leadership was critical and the demonstrative effect important, and that governments should aggressively investigate and prosecute money launderers and companies that evade taxes. ; "For a continent that needs substantial financial resources to meet its development needs, we should celebrate our accountability agencies, the auditor general, the chief justice and the media to support the collective effort." ; Asked for more integrity and transparency among leaders and officials of public and private institutions through asset declarations, and urged African countries to sign up to international tax information treaties to enable exchange of information. ; "Countries should also build human and technological capacities of agencies tasked with tackling Illicit financial flows, and institute information sharing and collaboration between relevant government agencies and ministries." ; Applauded countries that have ratified existing global and continental initiatives on halting illicit financial flows.

a169.speaker: Report of President Mbeki's high-level panel on illicit financial flows
a169.name: Report of President Mbeki's high-level panel on illicit financial flows
a169.speech: According to the report, the continent loses between USD 50 billion and USD 80 billion a year due to illicit financial flows.

a169.speaker: United Nations (estimates)
a169.name: United Nations (estimates)
a169.speech: UN estimates that the amount Africa loses through illicit financial flows is roughly double the Official Development Assistance that Africa receives, and also outweighs the USD 42 billion that the continent received in Foreign Direct Investment in 2017.

a439.speaker: Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, President of Brazil
a439.name: Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva
a439.title: President of Brazil
a439.speech: "We have the responsibility to do better. It is with that hope that I hand the gavel of the G20 presidency to President Ramaphosa. This is not an ordinary handover of the presidency. It is the concrete expression of the historical, social and cultural ties that unite Latin America and Africa." ; wished Ramaphosa success in leading the G20 and said Brazil is available to help South Africa exercise a presidency that goes beyond the previous one ; "I recall the words of another great South African, Nelson Mandela, who said: It is easy to demolish and destroy, the heroes are those who build. Let us continue building a just world and a sustainable planet."

a731.speaker: Equality Court (judgment)
a731.name: Equality Court (judgment)
a731.speech: Advised ANC Youth League leader Julius Malema to be wary, in the words of Oliver Wendell Holmes, of turning into "a man who often speaks but seldom talks."

a731.speaker: Equality Court (judgment)
a731.name: Equality Court (judgment)
a731.speech: Found that when Malema had told a group of students that the woman who accused Jacob Zuma of rape must have enjoyed herself because she stayed for breakfast and asked for taxi money, he engaged in hate speech; because he had not expressed an opinion or comment, but professed to be stating facts (which he got wrong), that hate speech does not enjoy protection in terms of the constitutional provision for freedom of expression, which leaves him liable. Ordered that he has two weeks to issue a public apology and one month to donate R50,000 to People Opposed to Women Abuse (Powa).

a731.speaker: Equality Court (judgment)
a731.name: Equality Court (judgment)
a731.speech: Found that Malema was speaking to the broader South African society, on which he has significant influence, especially when it comes to young people, rather than just to the students at the rally in Cape Town who were physically present, meaning that regardless of how those students interpreted his statements, they need to be judged on how any person on the street would react to them. Rejected Malema's argument that both he, and the ANC in general, work towards the empowerment of women.

a731.speaker: Julius Malema, ANC Youth League leader
a731.name: Julius Malema
a731.title: ANC Youth League leader
a731.speech: Told the court during hearings last year that he would comply with both instructions (a public apology and the R50,000 donation) if found guilty ; argued that both he, and the ANC in general, work towards the empowerment of women.

a731.speaker: Lisa Vetten, expert researcher and councillor on violence against women, called by the Sonke Gender Justice Network
a731.name: Lisa Vetten
a731.title: expert researcher and councillor on violence against women, called by the Sonke Gender Justice Network
a731.speech: Told the court that Malema had engaged in myth-making by trying to set out the parameters of what does (and does not) constitute rape. Doing so, she said, reinforces the idea that women lie about rape and creates the notion that men have no obligation to obtain explicit consent from women before sex; instead consent can be inferred based on the behaviour of the woman after the fact, which raises a whole host of dangers.

a802.speaker: Brigadier General Zibrim Bawah Ayorrogo, Commissioner General of the Customs Division of the Ghana Revenue Authority (GRA)
a802.name: Brigadier General Zibrim Bawah Ayorrogo
a802.title: Commissioner General of the Customs Division of the Ghana Revenue Authority (GRA)
a802.speech: Said the initiative was a significant milestone for the Customs Division and Customs Administration across the region ; "The introduction of the AEO Programme into the supply chain in Customs worldwide began after the September 11 terrorist attack in the US. The attacks significantly impacted global trade, highlighting the need for supply chain security. In response to the impact of the attack, the USAID initiated measures to secure supply chains, including partnerships between Customs Administration and supply chain operators" ; said the partnerships aimed to implement security measures according to Customs Standards, conduct audits to ensure compliance, recognise certified operators with special status, and provide benefits such as faster clearance and information sharing; however, he said implementing those measures posed significant challenges for Customs, requiring a balance between trade facilitation and supply chain security.

a802.speaker: Brigadier General Zibrim Bawah Ayorrogo, Commissioner General of the Customs Division of the GRA
a802.name: Brigadier General Zibrim Bawah Ayorrogo
a802.title: Commissioner General of the Customs Division of the GRA
a802.speech: "The WCO responded by designing the Safe Framework of Standards to secure and facilitate global trade in 2005. A key tool within the framework is the AEO concept, which is pillar two of the Safe Framework, designated as Customs Business Operations" ; "The Customs Business Operations foster partnerships between Customs Administration and the supply chain operators by establishing safety and security standards, operators voluntarily accepting and implementing these standards, Customs auditing for compliance, rewarding certified operators with benefits like fast clearance, information sharing, reduced control, priority of treatment" ; said the legal provisions governing the AEO Programme were provided under Section 8 of the Customs Act 2015, Act 891 and Regulation 15 of the Customs Regulation 2015-2016-LI-2248, Article 7.7 of the World Trade Organisation Agreement on Trade Facilitation and the revised Kyoto Convention.

a802.speaker: Brigadier General Zibrim Bawah Ayorrogo, Commissioner General of the Customs Division of the GRA
a802.name: Brigadier General Zibrim Bawah Ayorrogo
a802.title: Commissioner General of the Customs Division of the GRA
a802.speech: Said the AEO programme was the future of Customs Administration as it integrated trade facilitation, supply chain security and compliance, thereby benefiting all stakeholders ; "This forward-looking approach addresses the complexities of international trade while tackling growing concerns around security, efficiency and global collaboration. As Customs Administration modernises, the AEO Programme plays a crucial role in building a more secure, efficient and resilient global trade environment. Most importantly, the AEO programme significantly enhances revenue mobilisation and revenue assurance for Customs Administration"

a802.speaker: Brigadier General Zibrim Bawah Ayorrogo, Commissioner General of the Customs Division of the GRA
a802.name: Brigadier General Zibrim Bawah Ayorrogo
a802.title: Commissioner General of the Customs Division of the GRA
a802.speech: On behalf of the division, expressed gratitude to the GRA Board and Club Management, GhanaLink Network Services, the GIZ Trade Hub Project, and the USAID Field Future Project for providing the necessary assistance for the successful implementation of the AEO Programme.

a802.speaker: Dan Neur, Head of the Tax Policy Unit of the Ministry of Finance
a802.name: Dan Neur
a802.title: Head of the Tax Policy Unit of the Ministry of Finance
a802.speech: Said it was a major milestone in "our collective efforts to enhance trade facilitation and security and compliance"; he said the certification was a testament to their dedication to facilitating legitimate trade while preventing illicit activities.

a802.speaker: Kyeremeh Yeboah, Head of Trade Facilitation at the Ministry of Trade and Industry
a802.name: Kyeremeh Yeboah
a802.title: Head of Trade Facilitation at the Ministry of Trade and Industry
a802.speech: Said he was glad that the Customs of Ghana had chalked up such a success; he said the ministry would duly inform the WTO about the operationalisation of the AEO.

a802.speaker: Nabali Bawa, Managing Director of Ghana Link Network Services (address read on his behalf)
a802.name: Nabali Bawa
a802.title: Managing Director of Ghana Link Network Services (address read on his behalf)
a802.speech: Said the initiative aligned perfectly with the country's vision of becoming a leading trade hub in West Africa.

a802.speaker: Bismark Kissi, AEO Project Manager and acting Deputy Commissioner in charge of Mining Operations (Customs)
a802.name: Bismark Kissi
a802.title: AEO Project Manager and acting Deputy Commissioner in charge of Mining Operations (Customs)
a802.speech: Said six more companies were expected to be certified by January 1, 2025.

a835.speaker: Melvin Foote, congressional advocate for the interests of Africa in the United States, founder and President of the Constituency for Africa
a835.name: Melvin Foote
a835.title: congressional advocate for the interests of Africa in the United States, founder and President of the Constituency for Africa
a835.speech: Urges Liberia to strengthen its regional partnerships in light of the U.S. Government's freeze of foreign assistance ; Says it would be even more crucial for Liberia to explore new partnerships regionally and internationally to fill the gap left by the U.S. freeze, noting that strengthening relationships with neighboring countries and regional organizations like ECOWAS and the African Union could provide new opportunities for trade, security cooperation, and development projects ; Stresses that Liberia might need to prioritize building more substantial domestic capacity and local solutions to reduce dependency on foreign aid.

a835.speaker: Melvin Foote, congressional advocate for the interests of Africa in the United States
a835.name: Melvin Foote
a835.title: congressional advocate for the interests of Africa in the United States
a835.speech: "Last week, the United States government froze nearly all foreign assistance worldwide," he recounts, indicating a rethink of strategies.

a835.speaker: Melvin Foote, congressional advocate for the interests of Africa in the United States
a835.name: Melvin Foote
a835.title: congressional advocate for the interests of Africa in the United States
a835.speech: "The current freeze on aids, through USAID, must be seen as a wakeup call for African leaders to work together to reduce the impacts such decision may have on the continent," he notes.

a835.speaker: Melvin Foote, founder and President of the Constituency for Africa
a835.name: Melvin Foote
a835.title: founder and President of the Constituency for Africa
a835.speech: Lauds President Boakai for efforts to improve governance in Liberia.

a835.speaker: Melvin Foote, congressional advocate for the interests of Africa in the United States
a835.name: Melvin Foote
a835.title: congressional advocate for the interests of Africa in the United States
a835.speech: Argues that the ongoing freeze on aid worldwide by the United States government is having an unprecedented humanitarian impact on millions worldwide.

a835.speaker: Melvin Foote, congressional advocate for the interests of Africa in the United States
a835.name: Melvin Foote
a835.title: congressional advocate for the interests of Africa in the United States
a835.speech: Is optimistic that countries like Liberia stand a chance of weaving out the opportunities if they form strong partnerships with counterparts on the continent.

a926.speaker: Ethiopian Customs Commission (ECC) data
a926.name: Ethiopian Customs Commission (ECC) data
a926.speech: According to data from the Ethiopian Customs Commission (ECC), before the suspension of the tariff, the total volume of cut flowers supplied to the UK market accounted for 7.8pc, estimated at 41.1 million dollars in value; no positive change has been recorded after introducing zero tariffs, with market share declining to six percent in September and five percent in October 2024.

a926.speaker: An exporter with a farm in the Bishoftu (Debre Zeit) cluster, Oromia Regional State (anonymous)
a926.name: An exporter with a farm in the Bishoftu (Debre Zeit) cluster
a926.title: Oromia Regional State (anonymous)
a926.speech: Said the problem is not about overlooking the advantage of the tariff suspension but the long-term sales contract agreements made with UK retailers and supermarkets before the suspension.

a926.speaker: Another exporter operating in central Ethiopia (anonymous)
a926.name: Another exporter operating in central Ethiopia (anonymous)
a926.speech: Found selling price negotiations in UK retail shops and supermarkets costly; he experienced that negotiations with buyers in different market segments are time-consuming and resource-intensive and may not always lead to a favourable outcome.

a926.speaker: Several other flower farms operating in different horticulture clusters
a926.name: Several other flower farms operating in different horticulture clusters
a926.speech: Would argue that the suspension favoured 19 African countries that are members of the Commonwealth of Nations; exporters consider Ethiopia's non-membership of this bloc a factor that limits them from optimising the benefit of the UK's tariff suspension.

a1078.speaker: Somali government officials
a1078.name: Somali government officials
a1078.speech: Say the new tax law introduced at the annual tax forum will modernize revenue collection and reduce the country's reliance on foreign aid.

a1078.speaker: Somali government representative (anonymous)
a1078.name: Somali government representative (anonymous)
a1078.speech: "This new tax law is a crucial component of our efforts to build a stronger and more self-reliant Somalia." ; "By streamlining our tax processes and improving collection, we can generate the necessary resources to invest in services that our people deserve."

a1078.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a1078.name: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a1078.speech: Has long pressed Somalia to modernize customs administration and broaden its tax base beyond the narrow revenues collected at Mogadishu's port and airport; its program requires the government to strengthen domestic revenue mobilization.

a1078.speaker: Business leaders at the forum
a1078.name: Business leaders at the forum
a1078.speech: Welcomed the reforms but called for transparency and predictability in implementation. They argued that a fair tax system would boost investor confidence and create a more stable environment for private sector growth.

a1078.speaker: Somali officials
a1078.name: Somali officials
a1078.speech: Say raising domestic revenue is critical to delivering services and building resilience, with more than 7 million Somalis in need of aid.

a1078.speaker: Somali officials
a1078.name: Somali officials
a1078.speech: Pledged to continue consultations with the private sector as the law is rolled out, describing the forum's conclusion as a milestone in Somalia's effort to fortify financial institutions and lay the foundation for sustainable economic development.

a1115.speaker: Dr. Jean Kaseya, Director-General of Africa CDC (statement released on January 31, 2025)
a1115.name: Dr. Jean Kaseya
a1115.title: Director-General of Africa CDC (statement released on January 31, 2025)
a1115.speech: "This is not just an African problem; it is a global crisis in the making," warned Dr. Jean Kaseya. "We are at risk of losing everything we fought for over the past two decades."

a1115.speaker: Dr. Jean Kaseya, Director-General of Africa CDC
a1115.name: Dr. Jean Kaseya
a1115.title: Director-General of Africa CDC
a1115.speech: On Goma and eastern DRC: "I will personally fly there to ensure these life-saving interventions reach those in need—but we must have safe access."

a1115.speaker: Dr. Jean Kaseya, Director-General of Africa CDC
a1115.name: Dr. Jean Kaseya
a1115.title: Director-General of Africa CDC
a1115.speech: Emphasized that aid alone will not be enough and that the region's leaders must act decisively to end conflicts that are fueling disease outbreaks: "To my fellow African leaders: End this unnecessary war. If you fail to act, it will not be bullets that kill us—it will be major outbreaks and pandemics emerging from this region, devastating economies and sparing no one."

a1151.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State
a1151.name: Marco Rubio
a1151.title: US Secretary of State
a1151.speech: Praised the leadership of King Mohammed VI in promoting regional and international peace and security; in a statement released on Monday 27 January 2025 in Washington following a telephone conversation with Nasser Bourita, Minister of Foreign Affairs, African Cooperation and Moroccans Residing Abroad, he underlined the importance of the Moroccan-American strategic partnership in favour of regional and international peace and security, praising the King's leadership in this context.

a1151.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State
a1151.name: Marco Rubio
a1151.title: US Secretary of State
a1151.speech: Conveyed the United States' willingness to intensify cooperation with Morocco in order to advance common interests in the region and to put an end to conflicts, notably within the framework of the Abraham Accords.

a1151.speaker: Spokesperson of the US State Department (statement)
a1151.name: Spokesperson of the US State Department (statement)
a1151.speech: Indicated that the discussions between the two parties also covered the implementation of the ceasefire agreement in Gaza, the release of the hostages, as well as Morocco's leadership in delivering humanitarian aid to the Palestinians.

a1151.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State, and Nasser Bourita, Moroccan Minister of Foreign Affairs, African Cooperation and Moroccans Residing Abroad
a1151.name: Marco Rubio
a1151.title: US Secretary of State, and Nasser Bourita, Moroccan Minister of Foreign Affairs, African Cooperation and Moroccans Residing Abroad
a1151.speech: Stressed the importance of strengthening trade and investment between the two countries for the benefit of both peoples, the State Department statement concludes.

a1153.speaker: Abdoulaye Diop, Mali's Foreign Minister
a1153.name: Abdoulaye Diop
a1153.title: Mali's Foreign Minister
a1153.speech: Said of the Moscow consultations that "the consultations demonstrated that Russia and the Sahel countries share a common vision of their international obligations, obligations based on respect for the sovereignty of our countries, respect for the sovereign choice of our countries, but also taking into account the interests of our peoples" and that the countries work internationally "to fight together against imperialism, neocolonialism, the subjugation of our countries, the instrumentalization of human rights, and the rejection of interference in the internal affairs of countries." ; Said they wanted to build a strategic partnership with Russia on peace and security, wanting Russia to "accompany the confederation mechanism by supporting joint military operations that we conduct on the ground, and then with the prospect of creating a joint force to contain this security threat"; said the third aspect was development, including infrastructure, railways, energy, agriculture, mineral resources and the creation of an investment bank; and said they had agreed to institutionalize the consultation mechanism to meet at least once a year, alternately in Russia and the Sahel region.

a1153.speaker: Abdoulaye Diop, Mali's Foreign Minister
a1153.name: Abdoulaye Diop
a1153.title: Mali's Foreign Minister
a1153.speech: On a possible Sahel-Russia summit, said "this is not excluded a priori, we have not openly discussed this issue, but the mechanism exists and depends on the will of our heads of state," adding that President Vladimir Putin and the heads of state of Burkina Faso, Niger and Mali "have a common vision of our problems" and consult regularly, and that he does not rule out that one day they will decide to meet.

a1153.speaker: Abdoulaye Diop, Mali's Foreign Minister
a1153.name: Abdoulaye Diop
a1153.title: Mali's Foreign Minister
a1153.speech: Said on arms autonomy that "we are already working with Russia on several projects" and that it is important that Russia "does not object to the transfer of technology and the strengthening of our production capacities"; said President Goita has ambitions to develop the military industry in Mali and that together with Russian companies and the Russian government they will be able to create military capacities and a military industry in the Sahel region, reducing dependence on imported military equipment while creating jobs.

a1153.speaker: Abdoulaye Diop, Mali's Foreign Minister
a1153.name: Abdoulaye Diop
a1153.title: Mali's Foreign Minister
a1153.speech: Said the visa issue is an initiative of the heads of state, that experts have analysed it and made proposals and that it is an ongoing project; said the AES passport and biometric identity card were adopted in January by Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger, meet technical standards going beyond the usual requirements of the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), and that ICAO and all interested states were notified and given physical samples of the ordinary, diplomatic and service passports.

a1153.speaker: Abdoulaye Diop, Mali's Foreign Minister
a1153.name: Abdoulaye Diop
a1153.title: Mali's Foreign Minister
a1153.speech: Said on language cooperation that "this is a goal that we welcome – for Russian experts or Russia as a state to decide to work with our countries to promote our languages," that the development of national languages is a political goal and top priority, and that they are not closed to the use of working languages – Russian, French or English; said cultural relations with Russia date back to the first years of independence, that thousands of Malians studied in the former USSR and now in Russia, and that they welcome and encourage the learning of Russian as it can contribute to mutual understanding and strengthen trade and cultural ties.

a1153.speaker: Abdoulaye Diop, Mali's Foreign Minister
a1153.name: Abdoulaye Diop
a1153.title: Mali's Foreign Minister
a1153.speech: On the termination of the USAID program, said "Personally, I am not shocked by this decision. Moreover, the Government of Mali was not shaken either." He said Mali had been negotiating with USAID for several months and the negotiations were extremely difficult and stalled "because the way American aid was distributed in Mali did not allow Malians to determine priorities themselves, choose NGOs to implement projects, and the funds allocated did not even pass through the state budget," and that Mali opposed this, guided by the principle of national sovereignty in matters of development. He said the second lesson is that "when these countries decide to suspend their aid overnight, it means that the aid was not provided to our peoples, but was a political tool or a foreign policy lever to achieve certain goals," and the third lesson is that "our countries must be realistic" and "cannot make our plans based on the interests of others." He said they must find mechanisms to finance their countries from domestic resources and identify international resources not subject to political dictates, including within BRICS or other associations.

a1153.speaker: Abdoulaye Diop, Mali's Foreign Minister
a1153.name: Abdoulaye Diop
a1153.title: Mali's Foreign Minister
a1153.speech: Said that "peace between Russia and Ukraine will be beneficial for the whole world, both for stability and for the global economy," that Mali supports it and urges Russia to continue its efforts, and that Mali expresses solidarity with Russia; said that Mali, which has severed relations with Ukraine, considers Ukraine "a terrorist state," that "Ukraine has openly declared its support for terrorist groups in the Sahel, especially in Mali, which has led to the deaths of many of our soldiers and citizens," that Ukraine "must bear responsibility" and that African peoples should consider it "a source of instability in our region, as an irresponsible player who poses a threat to our security"; added that if peace allows unhindered supply of Ukrainian and Russian products, including grain and fertilizers, to countries that need it "that's great," and that Mali and the AES support all initiatives leading to a just and lasting peace that takes into account Russia's legitimate security concerns.

a1215.speaker: African Union (AU)
a1215.name: African Union (AU)
a1215.speech: Has formally endorsed the "Correct The Map" campaign, which calls for the replacement of the Mercator map with the Equal Earth projection. According to the AU, Africa's true size is 30.37 million square kilometres (11.73 million square miles) and is big enough to fit Europe, China and the United States combined, with space left over. The AU has pledged to advocate for wider adoption of Equal Earth and discuss collective action with its 55 member states.

a1215.speaker: Selma Malika Haddadi, AU Commission Deputy Chairperson
a1215.name: Selma Malika Haddadi
a1215.title: AU Commission Deputy Chairperson
a1215.speech: "It might seem to be just a map, but in reality, it is not." ; She argued that when Africa is misrepresented in size, the world's perception of the continent is also distorted – in media, education and policy.

a1215.speaker: Campaigners ("Correct the Map" campaign)
a1215.name: Campaigners ("Correct the Map" campaign)
a1215.speech: Argue that this visual misrepresentation reinforces colonial-era narratives that portray Africa as marginal, underdeveloped and peripheral to global affairs.

a1215.speaker: Carlos Lopes, professor at the University of Cape Town and proponent of the "Correct the Map" campaign
a1215.name: Carlos Lopes
a1215.title: professor at the University of Cape Town and proponent of the "Correct the Map" campaign
a1215.speech: "Maps shape how we see ourselves and how others see us." ; "If Africa appears smaller than it is, so does its weight in the imagination of citizens and decision-makers. Correcting the map is not vanity – it is reclaiming reality."

a1215.speaker: Fara Ndiaye, Speak Up Africa co-founder
a1215.name: Fara Ndiaye
a1215.title: Speak Up Africa co-founder
a1215.speech: Noted the psychological impact of distorted maps on African children. "They grow up thinking Africa is modest in size when, in reality, it's gigantic—larger than the US, China, India, Japan and much of Europe combined. Perception translates into confidence and confidence into action."

a1215.speaker: Fara Ndiaye, Speak Up Africa co-founder
a1215.name: Fara Ndiaye
a1215.title: Speak Up Africa co-founder
a1215.speech: "It's the first time a pan-African institution has taken a clear position on the visual representation of Africa." ; This transforms a cultural and civic demand into a continental policy aimed at the entire world, he argued.

a1215.speaker: "Correct The Map" petition (Africa No Filter and Speak Up Africa)
a1215.name: "Correct The Map" petition (Africa No Filter and Speak Up Africa)
a1215.speech: "As Africa becomes increasingly central to solving global challenges, it is critical to represent its true scale. That's why the Correct The Map campaign calls on the United Nations, as the global leader in international cooperation, and the BBC, as a global leading international media organisation, to adopt the Equal Earth projection in their data, reports, and materials that include world maps" ; "With their influence, these institutions can set a new standard and encourage others to follow suit in ensuring Africa is represented accurately as a critical driver of global growth and development."

a1215.speaker: Donald Porusingazi, political analyst
a1215.name: Donald Porusingazi
a1215.title: political analyst
a1215.speech: Said the map debate is emblematic of a broader postcolonial reckoning – a push to rewrite Africa's place in the world not just through policy but through perception. "Maps are instruments of power and Africa is ready to redraw the lines."

a1342.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a1342.name: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a1342.speech: Called on the Nigerian government on Friday to engender transparency and accountability in the oil sector in order to ensure that the gains of subsidy removal are fully maximised.

a1342.speaker: Abebe Selassie, Head of the African Department at the IMF
a1342.name: Abebe Selassie
a1342.title: Head of the African Department at the IMF
a1342.speech: "We have been commending bold reforms by the government, but we need to see a little more transparency in the oil sector to ensure that fuel subsidy removal can result in more flow of resources into government coffers," he noted. He also said the IMF was impressed by the reforms undertaken by the Nigerian government to address macroeconomic imbalances in the country, and that the subsidy was taking "a very large" share of government tax revenues, thus hampering optimal delivery of social services.

a1342.speaker: Abebe Selassie, Head of the African Department at the IMF
a1342.name: Abebe Selassie
a1342.title: Head of the African Department at the IMF
a1342.speech: "So it's been really good to see the government taking these head on, and also beginning to roll out the third component of the reforms that we've been advocating for, that the government has been pursuing, which is to expand social protection to target generalised subsidies to help the most vulnerable," ; "This has all been very good to see, but more can be done, particularly on the latter front; expanding social protection and also enhancing a lot more transparency in the oil sector, so that the removal of subsidies does translate into flow of revenue into government budget. So, there's still a bit more work to do in these areas."

a1342.speaker: Olawale Edun, Nigeria's Finance Minister
a1342.name: Olawale Edun
a1342.title: Nigeria's Finance Minister
a1342.speech: Told a gathering of investors, fund managers and financial experts in Washington that a forensic audit of the state-owned NNPC is underway, adding that the government also plans to reconcile the books of the oil company to reposition it for efficient operations and service delivery. "The NNPC needs to come to the table with more dollar revenue," the minister said.

a1342.speaker: IMF regional economic outlook for sub-Saharan Africa (report)
a1342.name: IMF regional economic outlook for sub-Saharan Africa (report)
a1342.speech: Said public debt ratios in sub-Saharan Africa have broadly stabilised but remain elevated compared to the pre-COVID-19 period, with baseline projections implying continued regional debt stabilization - and even some reduction - but assuming that recent efforts to consolidate budgets are maintained and in some cases intensified. It added that interest payments and overall debt service as a share of revenues are high, both historically and compared with other regions, constraining critical development spending, and that vulnerabilities and uncertainty persist as unforeseen events - such as shocks to global growth, global financial conditions, and official development assistance, as well as instability, conflicts, commodity price shocks, and natural disasters - may increase debt ratios significantly. "Furthermore, tight external financing conditions may increase rollover risk, and debt restructuring, which is sometimes essential, is socially costly and dauntingly complex," the report said.

a1528.speaker: Statement released by Brazil (BRICS host)
a1528.name: Statement released by Brazil (BRICS host)
a1528.speech: Said Egypt and Ethiopia balked at the group's backing of South Africa for a permanent seat on the UN Security Council, after new members opposed parts of a previously approved plan to reform the body.

a1528.speaker: Mauro Vieira, Brazilian Foreign Minister
a1528.name: Mauro Vieira
a1528.title: Brazilian Foreign Minister
a1528.speech: Said at a press conference after the statement was released that the group is working to overcome the differences and could still reach consensus at its leaders summit in July.

a1528.speaker: BRICS foreign ministers (via Brazil's statement)
a1528.name: BRICS foreign ministers (via Brazil's statement)
a1528.speech: "Voiced serious concerns about the rise of unjustified unilateral protectionist measures," including "indiscriminate raising of reciprocal tariffs and non-tariff measures" ; the group "called upon all sides to take measures to defend free trade and multilateral trading system, with a view to addressing current trade challenges and fostering a favorable trade and investment environment for all," while avoiding mentioning Trump or the US by name.

a1557.speaker: Binti Ali Wardhere, Mogadishu resident who survived the 1993 battle
a1557.name: Binti Ali Wardhere
a1557.title: Mogadishu resident who survived the 1993 battle
a1557.speech: Remembers of the day of the battle: "That day was calm." ; "To this day, I still see the bodies scattered in the streets." ; "There was hot water running over my head. I thought to myself: 'Who opened the water pipe?'" — she then realised it was the blood of the person who had died on top of her.

a1557.speaker: Binti Ali Wardhere, Mogadishu resident who lost her husband, two sons and brother in the battle
a1557.name: Binti Ali Wardhere
a1557.title: Mogadishu resident who lost her husband, two sons and brother in the battle
a1557.speech: Feels that simply telling the story is not enough and that the devastation inflicted on Somali families like hers remains largely unacknowledged: "It was the Americans who destroyed my house, killed my husband, my two sons, and my brother, and left my family in lasting misery." ; "At the very least, they must admit what they have done and compensate us."

a1557.speaker: Ahmed Mohamed Hassan (Ahmed Five), Somali cameraman who filmed the battle
a1557.name: Ahmed Mohamed Hassan (Ahmed Five)
a1557.title: Somali cameraman who filmed the battle
a1557.speech: Tells the BBC: "Although this situation was completely different from the ones I had worked in before, I still decided to record these events and take on that responsibility." ; says that until he filmed him, neither the US nor Aideed knew pilot Michael Durant was being held ; "I handed the videotapes to a UN plane that flew daily from Mogadishu to Nairobi [in neighbouring Kenya]. The first report of the Mogadishu battle to reach the world was from the footage I recorded. At the time, I was working as a freelancer for CNN." ; "This is something I take pride in - though at the time, I didn't anticipate its impact."

a1557.speaker: Ahmed Mohamed Hassan (Ahmed Five), Somali cameraman
a1557.name: Ahmed Mohamed Hassan (Ahmed Five)
a1557.title: Somali cameraman
a1557.speech: On the Netflix documentary: "This time, Somalis were given the opportunity to share their account of events. It is crucial that both sides of the story are always told."

a1557.speaker: Michael Durant, US Black Hawk pilot captured in Mogadishu
a1557.name: Michael Durant
a1557.title: US Black Hawk pilot captured in Mogadishu
a1557.speech: Later told the BBC: "It was a huge gun battle. They say that 25 Somalis were killed by gunfire at crash site two, so that gives you some insight into how much shooting was going on."

a1557.speaker: Saida Omar Mohamud, Mogadishu resident in whose home US soldiers took cover
a1557.name: Saida Omar Mohamud
a1557.title: Mogadishu resident in whose home US soldiers took cover
a1557.speech: Remembers at least 10 US soldiers storming into the house, gathering everyone into the living room, ordering them not to move and turning it into an impromptu field hospital: "Although they were afraid, they made us scared as well. They turned our house into a stronghold." She named her daughter, born that day, Amina Rangers.

a1557.speaker: Netflix documentary publicity material
a1557.name: Netflix documentary publicity material
a1557.speech: According to the publicity, the documentary features "raw, immersive storytelling with first-person interviews from both sides of the Battle of Mogadishu".

a1598.speaker: Ettie Higgins, UNICEF's deputy representative in Lebanon
a1598.name: Ettie Higgins
a1598.title: UNICEF's deputy representative in Lebanon
a1598.speech: told reporters in Geneva via video link from Beirut on Friday that U.S. aid cuts have forced UNICEF to suspend or scale back many programmes in Lebanon: "We have been forced to suspend or cut back or drastically reduce many of our programmes and that includes nutrition programmes" ; "The assessment revealed a grim picture of children's nutrition situation, particularly in the Baalbeck and Bekaa governorates, which remained densely populated when they were repeatedly targeted by air strikes" ; "More than half a million children and their families (in Lebanon) risk losing critical cash support from U.N. agencies this month. These cuts would strip the most vulnerable of their last lifeline, leaving them unable to afford even the most basic necessities."

a1598.speaker: UNICEF report
a1598.name: UNICEF report
a1598.speech: According to a UNICEF report that studied the impact of 14 months of hostilities between Hezbollah and Israel that began in October 2023, more than double the number of children faced food shortages in the eastern Bekaa and Baalbek regions of the country compared to two years ago; the report found nearly 80% of families were in need of urgent support and 31 per cent of households did not have enough drinking water, putting them at risk of disease.

a1598.speaker: UNICEF
a1598.name: UNICEF
a1598.speech: raised alarm about the impact of U.S. aid cuts and a broader decline in global humanitarian funding; only 26% of UNICEF's 2025 Lebanon appeal is funded.

a1598.speaker: Trump administration
a1598.name: Trump administration
a1598.speech: On Wednesday his administration said it was cutting more than 90% of the U.S. Agency for International Development's aid contracts.

a1604.speaker: Officials from the five African countries (unnamed, speaking to AFP)
a1604.name: Officials from the five African countries (unnamed
a1604.title: speaking to AFP)
a1604.speech: Have told AFP that they expect talks to centre on trade, investment and security, amongst other topics as they meet in the executive mansion's State Dining Room.

a1604.speaker: Trump administration
a1604.name: Trump administration
a1604.speech: Celebrated the formal shuttering of the US foreign aid agency USAID, trumpeting the move as an end to the "charity-based model."

a1604.speaker: Kula Fofana, press secretary to Liberian President Joseph Boakai
a1604.name: Kula Fofana
a1604.title: press secretary to Liberian President Joseph Boakai
a1604.speech: Told AFP on Tuesday that Liberia's president Joseph Boakai accepted the invitation with an eye on no longer being "solely (an) aid recipient". "Our interest is to look more to trade and engagement partners who will invest," she said.

a1604.speaker: Theophane Biyoghe, Gabonese presidential spokesman
a1604.name: Theophane Biyoghe
a1604.title: Gabonese presidential spokesman
a1604.speech: Said the meeting marked a chance for synergies "centred around the industrialisation of our economy."

a1604.speaker: Government of Guinea-Bissau
a1604.name: Government of Guinea-Bissau
a1604.speech: Said in April that it had turned over four convicted Latin American drug smugglers to the US DEA drug enforcement authority.

a1604.speaker: Umaro Sissoco Embalo, President of Guinea-Bissau
a1604.name: Umaro Sissoco Embalo
a1604.title: President of Guinea-Bissau
a1604.speech: Described the visit to the press as "very important" for his country. "Economically, this is a great opportunity opening for us," he declared, adding that he hoped his country would also benefit from "the support" the United States provides to other countries.

a1604.speaker: Karoline Leavitt, White House Press Secretary
a1604.name: Karoline Leavitt
a1604.title: White House Press Secretary
a1604.speech: Shared few details about the meeting when she told a briefing on Monday only that Trump would "host leaders of five African nations for lunch" in the State Dining Room.

a1666.speaker: Hadi Hallabi, Vice President, Government Services and International Trade Division
a1666.name: Hadi Hallabi
a1666.title: Vice President, Government Services and International Trade Division
a1666.speech: Praised the achievements of this tool, a genuine instrument for modernising the means of fighting fraud at the customs cordon. "We are pleased to bring a clear system here to Cotonou."

a1666.speaker: Boni Yayi, President of Benin (Head of State)
a1666.name: Boni Yayi
a1666.title: President of Benin (Head of State)
a1666.speech: First thanked participants for attending. Speaking of the reforms, he stated that they are among the priorities of his new five-year term and were indeed included in his manifesto, and that within this vast programme the port reforms are a key target. He specified that more than 100 billion had been invested by the MCC for the modernisation of the port and 200 billion by the Bolloré group. He did not hesitate to say "the competitiveness of the port is more than assured" with this project, and concluded: "We are convinced that our march towards emergence has already begun."

a1893.speaker: Dr Mololo Noah, One Health Coordinator, Office of the Prime Minister of Tanzania
a1893.name: Dr Mololo Noah
a1893.title: One Health Coordinator, Office of the Prime Minister of Tanzania
a1893.speech: "There has been a large increase in the indiscriminate use of ARVs to fatten chickens and pigs, a situation that contributes to the consumer suffering the harm of drug resistance because of the abundance of pathogen residues in the meat," he said. However, he said they still do not have statistics because they are continuing to carry out research and are now in a region-by-region campaign which, when completed, will give them the full picture and they will issue a report. He said that because of this challenge, the health sector is continuing with control efforts and providing education to citizens to abandon incorrect use ; "When we humans eat meat and eggs where the producer used drugs to fatten the livestock, one acquires drug resistance," he said, adding that to reach the goals of fighting this situation the Government has come up with a comprehensive campaign called 'Holehole itakucost' aimed at educating the community.

a1893.speaker: Muhimbili University of Health and Allied Sciences (Muhas) study, cited by Mwananchi on 13 September 2024
a1893.name: Muhimbili University of Health and Allied Sciences (Muhas) study
a1893.title: cited by Mwananchi on 13 September 2024
a1893.speech: Showed that 5.8 percent of people living with HIV and taking medication face the problem of pathogen resistance to the drugs that suppress that virus.

a1893.speaker: Dr Doreen Kamori, Senior Researcher, Microbiology and Immunology Unit, Muhimbili University of Health and Allied Sciences (Muhas)
a1893.name: Dr Doreen Kamori
a1893.title: Senior Researcher, Microbiology and Immunology Unit, Muhimbili University of Health and Allied Sciences (Muhas)
a1893.speech: Said they carried out that research in 2020 in 22 regions of Mainland Tanzania. She said the factors contributing to that problem include the importation into the country of drugs that contribute to resistance, and people not being good adherents in taking medication. Besides ARVs being used to fatten livestock and bringing drug resistance, she said other drugs being used are antibiotics ; "That is why we encourage health service providers to observe the laws on dispensing drugs by following the instructions of health professionals and the doctor's instructions when they serve patients," she said.

a1893.speaker: Dr Emmanuel Bahemana, Project Director, HJFMRI, Southern Highlands Regions
a1893.name: Dr Emmanuel Bahemana
a1893.title: Project Director, HJFMRI, Southern Highlands Regions
a1893.speech: Said the indiscriminate use of ARVs has caused an average of 3.9 to 19.3 percent of people living with HIV to be found to have resistance to the new antiretroviral drug Dolutegravir (DTG). "Indiscriminate use and the eating of meat products raised with ARVs has caused drug resistance despite various efforts to change the drugs of people living with HIV, but because of this situation there is a concern that there will be large numbers of patients found with resistance in the days ahead," he said. He said that if appropriate steps to control the indiscriminate use of drugs are not taken there is a great possibility of a large increase in HIV infections and a reduction in the workforce. "The new drug DTG two years ago was able to perform well in the fight against HIV but because of indiscriminate use an average of 3.9 to 19.3 percent of people using drugs to suppress HIV infection have been found to have drug resistance," he said ; because of this situation, he said they have been compelled to hold a joint conference involving the livestock and health sectors, researchers and scientists in order to seek a remedy for controlling the indiscriminate use of ARVs to fatten animal products.

a1893.speaker: Dr Chacha Mangu, Ministry of Health, Preventive Department, Disease Control Unit
a1893.name: Dr Chacha Mangu
a1893.title: Ministry of Health, Preventive Department, Disease Control Unit
a1893.speech: Said a major challenge has emerged of the indiscriminate use of human drugs on animals, causing resistance of disease pathogens that do not respond to treatment. He said various studies have been carried out in the country and have shown a large increase in the use of ARVs causing resistance of disease pathogens to the drugs ; "This conference is one of the meetings to discuss health matters, diseases involving humans, animals and the environment, with the aim of discussing the challenges of the indiscriminate use of drugs, especially ARVs, and coming up with joint strategies," he said.

a1893.speaker: Rehema Mwanjonde, resident of Nonde in Mbeya city
a1893.name: Rehema Mwanjonde
a1893.title: resident of Nonde in Mbeya city
a1893.speech: Asked the Government through the Ministry of Health to put in place a special campaign against the indiscriminate use of drugs in order to save the current generation, especially those affected by new HIV infections. "We see stakeholders including the HJFMRI organisation, through the US President's Emergency Plan (Pepfar), how they are fighting the war against HIV to save the lives of Tanzanians. When it comes to a few people who for their personal interests do damage, let the law take its course," she said.

a1893.speaker: Dr Mpoki Alinanuswe, Officer-in-Charge, Tanzania Meat Board (TMB), Southern Highlands Zone
a1893.name: Dr Mpoki Alinanuswe
a1893.title: Officer-in-Charge, Tanzania Meat Board (TMB), Southern Highlands Zone
a1893.speech: Said the matter of ARVs fattening livestock is just like how they work in the human body, strengthening immunity and bringing an appetite to eat. "It is not that they have chemicals that can fatten an animal, because the nature of ARVs is to boost the body's immunity and help a person affected by HIV to increase their appetite and strengthen their health; that is the reason why when people consume the meat they suffer the effect of drug resistance in the body," he said. He advised the community to stop the use of ARVs to feed livestock in order to avoid harm to humans in failing to get proper treatment when they need medical services ; "I cannot say directly that ARVs have pathogens for fattening meat products, but their use in humans protects health and that is the same system in animals," he said.

a1958.speaker: The New York Times
a1958.name: The New York Times
a1958.speech: According to the New York Times, the passage of the bill would be the latest sign of a U.S. retreat from Africa, after Mr Trump’s slashing of foreign aid and introduction of unprecedented tariffs on the African continent.

a1958.speaker: Helen Dempster, policy fellow and assistant director for the Migration, Displacement, and Humanitarian Policy Programme at the Centre for Global Development
a1958.name: Helen Dempster
a1958.title: policy fellow and assistant director for the Migration, Displacement, and Humanitarian Policy Programme at the Centre for Global Development
a1958.speech: Said countries in Africa would be hit the hardest should the bill pass: “For the poorest people on the planet, they are going to be hit twice by the various different steps that the U.S. administration is taking,” Ms Dempster said in an interview with the New York Times.

a1958.speaker: Helen Dempster, policy fellow at the Centre for Global Development
a1958.name: Helen Dempster
a1958.title: policy fellow at the Centre for Global Development
a1958.speech: Noted that the bill intended to discourage people from relocating to the United States while forcing those in the country to consider self-deportation.

a1958.speaker: Kristi Noem, Homeland Security Secretary
a1958.name: Kristi Noem
a1958.title: Homeland Security Secretary
a1958.speech: Said the policy of offering a $1,000 stipend as travel assistance to migrants who deport themselves covered part of Mr Trump’s administration’s push to encourage immigrants to deport themselves as a way to help the president meet lofty immigration promises in the country.

a2082.speaker: Dr. Hodan Osman Abdi, Somalia's Ambassador to China
a2082.name: Dr. Hodan Osman Abdi
a2082.title: Somalia's Ambassador to China
a2082.speech: Told SONNA that Somalia's participation in the China-Africa Economic and Trade Expo marked a turning point in how Somalia presents itself to the world: "Many people believe Somalia has nothing to export, but this event challenges that narrative. It showed the world that Somali products have value and potential."

a2082.speaker: Xi Jinping, Chinese President
a2082.name: Xi Jinping
a2082.title: Chinese President
a2082.speech: Announced that imports from African countries with strong ties to China would be exempt from customs duties.

a2082.speaker: Dr. Hodan Osman Abdi, Somalia's Ambassador to China
a2082.name: Dr. Hodan Osman Abdi
a2082.title: Somalia's Ambassador to China
a2082.speech: Described Xi Jinping's customs duty exemption decision as "encouraging and central to enabling Somali exports to access Chinese markets."

a2082.speaker: Dr. Hodan Osman Abdi, Somalia's Ambassador to China
a2082.name: Dr. Hodan Osman Abdi
a2082.title: Somalia's Ambassador to China
a2082.speech: Highlighted the value of sustainable, long-term investment particularly in human development: "Financial aid and donations are important, especially in times of urgent need. But what truly builds a country's future is the ability to stand on its own through education, skills training, and institutional development." ; noted that China has increasingly prioritized capacity-building and scholarships for Somali students and professionals: "There's a well-known Chinese proverb that says: 'Giving someone a fish is not as good as teaching them how to fish.' That spirit reflects the depth of the relationship we're not just receiving help, we're being equipped to help ourselves."

a2082.speaker: Dr. Hodan Osman Abdi, Somalia's Ambassador to China
a2082.name: Dr. Hodan Osman Abdi
a2082.title: Somalia's Ambassador to China
a2082.speech: Highlighted Somalia's strategic importance in the modern Silk Road: "As China renews the Belt and Road Initiative, Somalia has a chance to become a key connector between the Indian Ocean, the Arab world, and the rest of Africa." ; concluded by reflecting on the 65-year journey of Somali-Chinese relations: "We must take advantage of this moment, to build a future where Somalia is no longer defined by crisis, but by its contributions and potential."

a2321.speaker: Sabine Dall'Omo, CEO of Siemens for Southern and Eastern Africa
a2321.name: Sabine Dall'Omo
a2321.title: CEO of Siemens for Southern and Eastern Africa
a2321.speech: "Siemens is active in all the countries on the African continent. My responsibility is for the Anglophone Africa plus islands to the Eastern side of the continent. Our main focus is on the electrification, automation and digitalization. When we talk about Africa, we know that electricity is the founding principle in order to access any further development in any of the countries." ; "So electricity and the supply of it to the consumer; be it private or industrial consumer, is our main focus in the business we are currently in but also in the context of specifically industrial applications, like for instance in the food processing side, in the pharmaceutical side our technology of automation is very crucial in order to ensure consistent productivity and products to come out." ; "Combined with digital application, and this is something we are very excited about looking into the future of Africa because the continent is much faster developing in the context of digital applications."

a2321.speaker: Sabine Dall'Omo, CEO of Siemens for Southern and Eastern Africa
a2321.name: Sabine Dall'Omo
a2321.title: CEO of Siemens for Southern and Eastern Africa
a2321.speech: "Maybe to demystify the past a bit, our activity in Africa, specifically in the early 2000's was very much around the telecommunication environment but in 2007 we basically merged our telecommunication business with Nokia so it's not part of our portfolio anymore. But many of the backbones of companies in the telecom industry were based on Siemen's technology." ; "When we look at Ethiopia; it is a great market for German industries, specifically also looking at possibilities to have cooperation with Germany and establishing how we can industrialize Ethiopia and having the benefit of the workforce available in Ethiopia. Therefore we have our own legal setup in Ethiopia which we opened last year in Addis Ababa."

a2321.speaker: Lukas Duursema, CEO of Siemens East Africa
a2321.name: Lukas Duursema
a2321.title: CEO of Siemens East Africa
a2321.speech: "In Ethiopia specifically we have decided to create an East African hub of which the headquarter office is based in Ethiopia. There are a few factors that led us to make that decision; one was growth potential opportunities and we have accessibility in the hub itself; as you know Ethiopian Airlines is well connected in the whole of East Africa, we also considered economic growth and Ethiopia is a nice place to be in." ; "We focus very strongly on electrification in Ethiopia, which is a core market. Electrification will continue for a number of years; if you look at the electrification plan that Ethiopia has set aside with the Grand Renaissance Dam being built and other projects to come as well, it is a core area for us." ; "We are currently executing the Ethiopia, Kenya interconnect project. Specifically on the automation side, if you look at both old and new projects that are being implemented, they are using Siemens automation technology, Siemens drives; both electrical and mechanical drives."

a2321.speaker: Sabine Dall'Omo, CEO of Siemens for Southern and Eastern Africa
a2321.name: Sabine Dall'Omo
a2321.title: CEO of Siemens for Southern and Eastern Africa
a2321.speech: "It might sound like a big area to cover but when we look into the Siemens philosophy, our values are always more than just the inherent business only, so we always look after the countries where we are present." ; "If I want to sell a product, say like a power plant, then I need to make sure I also take care of the infrastructure around it which is not only physical infrastructure, but also the people and the social development because when everything develops in a country then there is so much more potential for us to do business and for others." ; "For us what is absolutely crucial, specifically in the context of Africa, is to have strong partnerships in the countries, because at the end of the day, you want to develop a local economy." ; "Our view is also always to improve society, specifically on health, but also education to make sure that we also, later on, have the possibility to have the work force to work on our projects and work for our customer's projects."

a2321.speaker: Sabine Dall'Omo, CEO of Siemens for Southern and Eastern Africa
a2321.name: Sabine Dall'Omo
a2321.title: CEO of Siemens for Southern and Eastern Africa
a2321.speech: "Currently we are working with both [private and public sector]. If you take for example the Ethiopia, Kenya interconnection, we are working with a civil company which is basically a woman who has a private entity here in Ethiopia which is now basically our civil company executing this project." ; "In the public space we are definitely more engaged because most of the infrastructure projects are government funded projects and only the government will be able to put a value proposition later on for such kinds of projects."

a2321.speaker: Lukas Duursema, CEO of Siemens East Africa
a2321.name: Lukas Duursema
a2321.title: CEO of Siemens East Africa
a2321.speech: "If you also look our portfolio, some of it is facilitated out of a project, which means we have to sub-contract some components of it and some require local partners. So we do have a very strong partner focus to be able to have some of our portfolio. It provides opportunities for local entities and companies to develop new portfolios or projects that also help us expand our business." ; "We are currently in discussions with a number of local entities in Ethiopia, in addition to other countries, where we try to find out where we can fit them in to help us to generate business."

a2321.speaker: Sabine Dall'Omo, CEO of Siemens for Southern and Eastern Africa
a2321.name: Sabine Dall'Omo
a2321.title: CEO of Siemens for Southern and Eastern Africa
a2321.speech: "So far we are proud of the Ethiopia, Kenya interconnect because it shows the integration of countries specifically in East Africa and that just resonates very well with the European community because I do believe it is a great step from a technology point of view, but also from a country point of view." ; "The cooperation with the Ethiopian government specifically in helping us setting up our entity here, being active, these are also success stories for us, it also gives us a lot of confidence that we have partners here which are willing to work with us."

a2321.speaker: Sabine Dall'Omo, CEO of Siemens for Southern and Eastern Africa
a2321.name: Sabine Dall'Omo
a2321.title: CEO of Siemens for Southern and Eastern Africa
a2321.speech: "If you look at Ethiopia's growth specifically, one of the challenges is the inflow of hard currency. Getting the country into a position that it is able to produce more value which it can later export for hard currency in order to fund investment projects is a challenge because this is the current limiting factor. The lack of infrastructure at the end of the day is always the hindering point; if you look at for instance energy, water and transport, specifically when you are outside of the major capital, you can see that there is a great need in order to improve and industrialize the society so then there is a higher productivity." ; "We are thinking about how we can make input costs for infrastructure lower. We have seen in Africa, many countries have a view towards China... We see there is great competence on the Chinese side and it is also more affordable for African countries. In Ethiopia there is a strong Chinese alliance and Siemens is a big company in China as well, we have 60,000 employees there and we are currently trying to understand to what extent we could package European technology with Chinese solutions making it more affordable and Ethiopia in that case will be in the position to afford infrastructure projects faster."

a2474.speaker: Erica Y Carr, Acting Executive Secretary, USAID (email)
a2474.name: Erica Y Carr
a2474.title: Acting Executive Secretary, USAID (email)
a2474.speech: Sent an email that thanked staff for clearing out classified safes and personnel documents from a Washington DC office and told them to meet in the building's lobby for an all-day disposal event on Tuesday: "Shred as many documents first, and reserve the burn bags for when the shredder becomes available or needs a break" ; the email asked staff not to overfill the burn bags and label them with the words "SECRET" and "USAID (B/IO)" using permanent markers.

a2474.speaker: US State Department
a2474.name: US State Department
a2474.speech: Did not immediately return a request for comment.

a2474.speaker: Nikki Gamer, spokesperson, American Foreign Service Association (AFSA)
a2474.name: Nikki Gamer
a2474.title: spokesperson, American Foreign Service Association (AFSA)
a2474.speech: Told the BBC that the union, which represents USAID staff, was aware employees had been asked to shred documents.

a2474.speaker: American Foreign Service Association (AFSA)
a2474.name: American Foreign Service Association (AFSA)
a2474.speech: Said it was "alarmed" by the reports and warned that such documents "may be relevant to ongoing litigation regarding the termination of USAID employees and the cessation of USAID grants" ; noted that federal law dictates that government records must be preserved as they are "essential to transparency, accountability, and the integrity of the legal process" ; warned that "the unlawful destruction of federal records could carry serious legal consequences for anyone directed to act in violation of the law."

a2474.speaker: Experts (unnamed, speaking to the BBC)
a2474.name: Experts (unnamed
a2474.title: speaking to the BBC)
a2474.speech: Said the email sent by Carr did not contain some of the details traditionally found in a records disposal request, raising concerns about procedure.

a2474.speaker: Kel McClanahan, executive director of the National Security Counselors
a2474.name: Kel McClanahan
a2474.title: executive director of the National Security Counselors
a2474.speech: "There is no indication in this email order that any thought is being given to proper retention or even identifying which records can be destroyed and which records cannot" ; filed a complaint with the National Archives and Records Administration, asking them to "take immediate measures" to stop the destruction of records.

a2474.speaker: The White House
a2474.name: The White House
a2474.speech: Has argued that the agency's international programmes were a wasteful use of taxpayer dollars.

a2474.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State and acting head of USAID (post on X)
a2474.name: Marco Rubio
a2474.title: US Secretary of State and acting head of USAID (post on X)
a2474.speech: Announced on X that the administration was cancelling "83% of the programmes at USAID" ; "The 5200 contracts that are now cancelled spent tens of billions of dollars in ways that did not serve, (and in some cases even harmed), the core national interests of the United States."

a2504.speaker: Naana Jane Opoku-Agyemang, Vice President of Ghana
a2504.name: Naana Jane Opoku-Agyemang
a2504.title: Vice President of Ghana
a2504.speech: Called on African leaders to demonstrate strong collective will and take decisive action to ensure the successful implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), emphasising that the single market presents a transformative opportunity for Africa's economic growth but that its success depends on the commitment and collaboration of all stakeholders: "The success of the single market depends on our collective will and decisive action. We must accelerate progress to ensure that Africa's gains are realized for this generation and the future ones." ; "As we engage in today's sessions, I encourage all of us to collaborate, to exchange ideas and to push Africa closer to a fully integrated market." ; urged policymakers, business leaders, and development partners to prioritize cooperation, share ideas, and work towards the seamless integration of African economies, saying eliminating trade barriers, enhancing infrastructure, and investing in digital connectivity will be critical; reiterated that a successful single market will not only boost intra-African trade but also drive industrialisation, create jobs and position the continent as a competitive global economic player.

a2504.speaker: Naana Jane Opoku-Agyemang, Vice President of Ghana
a2504.name: Naana Jane Opoku-Agyemang
a2504.title: Vice President of Ghana
a2504.speech: Emphasised that Ghana's modernisation of its ports was aimed at boosting trade, while ongoing expansion of road and rural networks seeks to connect key economic zones: "Our airports are one of the best on the continent, I must admit. Our ports are being modernised to facilitate trade and we are expanding our road and rural networks to connect key economic zones." ; underscored Ghana's investments in energy infrastructure designed to provide reliable and affordable power to industries and households; commended President Mahama for his commitment to infrastructure development, describing it as a key driver of Ghana's economic transition; acknowledged that while progress had been made, there was still much to be done across Africa, and pointed to digital infrastructure as a critical area for investment, noting that mobile technology had already revolutionized financial inclusion across the continent.

a2504.speaker: Dr. Fatima El Sheikh, Secretary General of the Arab Bank for Economic Development in Africa (BADEA)
a2504.name: Dr. Fatima El Sheikh
a2504.title: Secretary General of the Arab Bank for Economic Development in Africa (BADEA)
a2504.speech: Said the institution has invested more than $15 billion in Africa to date, with the bulk of the funds directed towards infrastructure development, and pointed out that over 60% to 70% of BADEA's investments had been focused on key infrastructure projects across the continent: "We are proud of our efforts, especially in building essential transportation networks. Over 40 airports have been constructed, and we've developed what we call 'isolation liberation roads'-roads that connect landlocked countries to ports and facilitate access to the sea."

a2504.speaker: Dr. Fatima El Sheikh, Secretary General of the Arab Bank for Economic Development in Africa (BADEA)
a2504.name: Dr. Fatima El Sheikh
a2504.title: Secretary General of the Arab Bank for Economic Development in Africa (BADEA)
a2504.speech: Emphasised the bank's commitment to the continent's continued growth, outlining BADEA's new ambition for the next five years: "We have recently launched a five-year plan, with an allocation of $18 million, aimed at continuing our infrastructure development initiatives. The focus will be on building on our existing projects and ensuring that more African nations benefit from better connectivity and access to global markets."

a2508.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a2508.name: Donald Trump
a2508.title: US President
a2508.speech: Has said he will cut all future funding to South Africa over allegations that it was confiscating land and "treating certain classes of people very badly" ; wrote on his social media platform Truth Social: "I will be cutting off all future funding to South Africa until a full investigation of this situation has been completed!" ; he later said, in a briefing with journalists, that South Africa's "leadership is doing some terrible things, horrible things."

a2508.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, President of South Africa (post on X)
a2508.name: Cyril Ramaphosa
a2508.title: President of South Africa (post on X)
a2508.speech: "South Africa is a constitutional democracy that is deeply rooted in the rule of law, justice and equality. The South African government has not confiscated any land." He added that the only funding South Africa received from the US was through the health initiative Pepfar, which represented "17% of South Africa's HIV/Aids programme."

a2508.speaker: Elon Musk, Trump adviser (post on X)
a2508.name: Elon Musk
a2508.title: Trump adviser (post on X)
a2508.speech: Said the new law discriminated against white people: "Why do you have openly racist ownership laws?"

a2508.speaker: US government data
a2508.name: US government data
a2508.speech: The US allocated about $440m (£358m) in assistance to South Africa in 2023, according to US government data.

a2631.speaker: Bank of Cabo Verde (communiqué of last December)
a2631.name: Bank of Cabo Verde (communiqué of last December)
a2631.speech: Announced that it had decided to raise the main interest rates, with effect from 2 January of this year.

a2631.speaker: Josefá Barbosa, economist (opinion author)
a2631.name: Josefá Barbosa
a2631.title: economist (opinion author)
a2631.speech: Argues that the interest rate policy has significant economic and social consequences — the cost of money increases, public debt grows, investment falls, resulting in lower economic growth, rising unemployment, higher inflation, reduced purchasing power and worsening poverty and social inequality; and that the misalignment with European partners means Cape Verdeans pay higher credit rates than foreigners, so that the economic sectors and even the country’s banks are mostly under foreign control.

a2631.speaker: Josefá Barbosa, economist (opinion author)
a2631.name: Josefá Barbosa
a2631.title: economist (opinion author)
a2631.speech: Concludes that Cabo Verde needs to abandon the policy of high interest rates and modest growth, beginning a cycle of progressive reduction of the interest rate, expansion of production, increased exports, generation of employment and income, and reduction of poverty and social inequality; and that a promising strategy would be to diversify the economy and trading partners, exploring renewable energy, the blue economy, services and sustainable tourism.

a2631.speaker: Forecasts for 2025 (cited economic projections)
a2631.name: Forecasts for 2025 (cited economic projections)
a2631.speech: GDP growth in the Euro Area of only 1.9%; public debt of 312,202 million ECV, 105% of GDP; budget deficit of 1.8% of GDP; public financing needs of more than 30,000 million ECV; external reserves below six months of imports; debt service rising to 18,000 million ECV in 2025; and tax revenues covering only 60% of the budget.

a2826.speaker: Eduardo Samo Gudo, Director-General of Mozambique's National Institute of Health (INS)
a2826.name: Eduardo Samo Gudo
a2826.title: Director-General of Mozambique's National Institute of Health (INS)
