a2826.speech: “The issue of the reduction of funding for health at world level could have a devastating impact, because of the consequences of health systems, which in many countries are already fragile, facing even greater shortages than those we have already been facing,” said at the opening of the meeting of the CPLP Network of National Public Health Institutes in Maputo ; warned of the emergence of new diseases and the worsening of those that already exist, given the insufficiency of funds to halt them ; “The appeal is global, it is to the whole world; international society has to look at health as a priority and the social sectors must continue to be at the centre of attention of all global agendas.”

a2826.speaker: International and humanitarian aid organisations
a2826.name: International and humanitarian aid organisations
a2826.speech: Have shown concern, in recent months, over the proliferation of announcements of cuts in US international aid.

a2826.speaker: Félix Rosenberg, executive director of the CPLP network of national public health institutes
a2826.name: Félix Rosenberg
a2826.title: executive director of the CPLP network of national public health institutes
a2826.speech: Presented the same concern, indicating that the aid being withdrawn was essential for carrying out research to monitor, predict and treat disease outbreaks and epidemics around the world ; “At this meeting we will deal with great emphasis with the question of food and nutritional security, basically hunger, which is one of the great concerns in the world because it is surely one of the worst epidemics. Perhaps much worse than covid-19; it does not attract as much attention, but it is among the worst epidemics.”

a2826.speaker: World (global) public health institutes, meeting in Maputo
a2826.name: World (global) public health institutes
a2826.title: meeting in Maputo
a2826.speech: Ended their meeting on Thursday with calls for investment in public health, including in the training of professionals, to halt future pandemics that threaten the world, and for “solidarity” among countries in combating new diseases ; on the list of threats of future world pandemics, listed as concerns the spread of emerging viruses such as dengue and chikungunya on every continent, the worldwide increase in mpox cases, the increased frequency of outbreaks of haemorrhagic fevers in Africa — namely Ebola, Marburg and hantavirus — and the rapid spread of bacteria highly resistant to antimicrobials.

a3053.speaker: National Council for Food and Nutritional Security
a3053.name: National Council for Food and Nutritional Security
a3053.speech: According to the National Council for Food and Nutritional Security, a total of 148,000 people in Mozambique are in an emergency situation and in need of urgent humanitarian assistance.

a3053.speaker: Judite Mussacula, executive secretary of the Food and Nutritional Security Technical Secretariat (SETSAN)
a3053.name: Judite Mussacula
a3053.title: executive secretary of the Food and Nutritional Security Technical Secretariat (SETSAN)
a3053.speech: said the people in question are living in 66 districts assessed by SETSAN. "The research shows that, of the approximately two million people in the regions assessed, 144,000 are in an emergency situation and need support" ; added that in those regions 24,400 households were covered. She claimed that 114,000 children, aged between 6 and 59 months, "have been acutely malnourished in the last two months and need health care. We are making efforts to improve malnutrition indicators among children" ; recalled that last June, the government launched a new food security strategy aimed at reducing chronic child malnutrition, which has been exacerbated by climate change in recent years.

a3053.speaker: Roberto Albino, Agriculture Minister
a3053.name: Roberto Albino
a3053.title: Agriculture Minister
a3053.speech: said that over the last ten years, the rate of chronic malnutrition among children under five years of age has fallen from 43 per cent in 2013 to the current 37 per cent, a level still considered as very high when compared to World Health Organization (WHO) recommendations ; "The government strategies are focused on healthy and nutritious agriculture on a scale that can solve the country's food problem."

a3059.speaker: Hopwood, analyst
a3059.name: Hopwood
a3059.title: analyst
a3059.speech: Said the budget will likely only pass the National Council, where a second round of debates is scheduled, by the end of May ; "It will have a negative effect on the implementation of the budget because the financial year has already started on 1 April. By the time the budget is passed by the National Council, it may well be the end of May" ; explained that the delay has resulted in offices, ministries and agencies (OMAs) having no clear guidelines on what their spending limits are ; "This means that OMAs will not be operating on the new spending levels until then. Ideally, we should switch to passing the budget at the end of the calendar year so that the financial year starts on January 1 or February 1 at the latest" ; "This would lead to more accurate spending of the budget and less likelihood that funds will be returned to the treasury unspent."

a3059.speaker: Evalistus Kaaronda, Swanu lawmaker
a3059.name: Evalistus Kaaronda
a3059.title: Swanu lawmaker
a3059.speech: Said the budget lacked clarity in terms of how the government would utilise money availed to it by finance minister Ericah Shafudah ; "The Appropriation Bill consists only of one single-page document with a list of amounts allocated to ministries and agencies. The ministerial budget statement lays out the thinking behind the amounts but does not define how the money will be raised, the risks involved and how each ministry will spend the allocated amounts."

a3059.speaker: Evalistus Kaaronda, Swanu lawmaker
a3059.name: Evalistus Kaaronda
a3059.title: Swanu lawmaker
a3059.speech: "External borrowing, especially the Eurobond, for instance, is due for [payment] later this year. What were the terms of borrowing and how do we reduce the appetite for borrowing? The mid-term review budget - the fiscal policy arrangements were not given together with the budget. Some of these are being electronically shared with us. We have not heard or received anything after the minister recalled what she shared with parliament."

a3059.speaker: Ministry of Finance of Namibia (statement)
a3059.name: Ministry of Finance of Namibia (statement)
a3059.speech: Said it has made all the relevant documents available to allow debates to start around the budget ; "As you are aware, the minister of finance tabled the budget duly upon the entry of the eighth administration. Prior to that, as well as subsequently, much work has gone in to align the budget with the policy ambitions of new frameworks such as National Development Plan 6 whilst also providing to the new members of parliament the required informative briefs on various aspects thereto" ; "The ministry of finance is working to ensure that the National Assembly is fully prepared to resume the debate on 8 April 2025."

a3061.speaker: Yusuf Tuggar, Nigerian Minister of Foreign Affairs
a3061.name: Yusuf Tuggar
a3061.title: Nigerian Minister of Foreign Affairs
a3061.speech: Expressed his country's refusal, declaring: "We have enough problems of our own (...) It would be unfair for us to accept 300 deported Venezuelans" ; denounced "considerable pressure exerted by the United States" for his country to accept individuals, some of whom have come "straight out of prison".

a3061.speaker: Donald Trump, President of the United States
a3061.name: Donald Trump
a3061.title: President of the United States
a3061.speech: Presented the presidents of Liberia, Senegal, Guinea-Bissau, Mauritania and Gabon, at a White House meeting, with a plan to relocate migrants to their territories.

a3061.speaker: US State Department document (reported by the Wall Street Journal)
a3061.name: US State Department document (reported by the Wall Street Journal)
a3061.speech: A State Department document sent ahead of the meeting called on these countries to accept the "dignified, safe and timely transfer from the United States" of third-country nationals, with a commitment not to send them back "to their country of origin or country of residence until a final decision has been made" on their asylum claims in the United States.

a3061.speaker: African leaders who attended the White House meeting
a3061.name: African leaders who attended the White House meeting
a3061.speech: Made no public comment after the meeting, but some are reportedly afraid of sanctions if they refused to cooperate, in particular the addition of their countries to the list of those already subject to a US entry ban.

a3061.speaker: United Nations
a3061.name: United Nations
a3061.speech: Fears a resumption of the civil war in South Sudan, the country to which eight undocumented migrants were deported in early July.

a3061.speaker: US administration
a3061.name: US administration
a3061.speech: Maintains, with the backing of the Supreme Court since June, that it has the power to deport foreign nationals to third countries if their country of origin refuses to take them back.

a3118.speaker: EFE (news agency reports)
a3118.name: EFE (news agency reports)
a3118.speech: According to reports by news agency EFE, heavy gunfire was seen on Friday near Haiti's national palace in its capital of Port-au-Prince, in the midst of political turmoil sparked by Prime Minister Ariel Henry's absence.

a3118.speaker: United States
a3118.name: United States
a3118.speech: Earlier this week called on Haiti's prime minister to expedite a political transition as armed gangs seek his ouster.

a3228.speaker: Ismail Omar Guelleh, President of Djibouti
a3228.name: Ismail Omar Guelleh
a3228.title: President of Djibouti
a3228.speech: The government officially launched the third phase of the national drought response plan in response to the solemn appeal of President Ismail Omar Guelleh; the solemn launch falls within the continuity of the efforts carried out over several months under the impetus of the President of the Republic.

a3228.speaker: Government of Djibouti
a3228.name: Government of Djibouti
a3228.speech: It should be noted that to date, including this new phase, the government expects to reach a total of 41,000 households benefiting from humanitarian assistance.

a3255.speaker: Dr. Pacqueens Aisagbonhi, UK-based educationist
a3255.name: Dr. Pacqueens Aisagbonhi
a3255.title: UK-based educationist
a3255.speech: Commended the National Association of Seadogs (Pyrates Confraternity) for its contribution to national development in addressing socio-economic challenges in the country, saying seadogs over the years has been empowering individuals and communities by promoting sustainable development practices in Nigeria: "The National Association of Seadogs has been involved in various activities aimed at contributing national development in Nigeria. Some of these contributions included advocacy for good governance by promoting transparency, accountability, and good governance. The association has been in the forefront of advocating for policies that enhance democratic processes and uphold the rule of law" ; Commended the association for its community development initiatives in the area of infrastructural improvement, education, healthcare, and sanitation in underserved communities across Nigeria, adding that such initiatives are aimed at uplifting local communities and improving their quality of life ; Urged the association to continue its humanitarian assistance by providing humanitarian aid to alleviate suffering and rebuild affected communities.

a3255.speaker: Brig. Gen. Samuel Oviawa (Rtd)
a3255.name: Brig. Gen. Samuel Oviawa (Rtd)
a3255.speech: In his paper titled "Combating Insecurity in Nigeria", said combating insecurity in Nigeria requires a multifaceted approach that involves the government, military, law enforcement agencies, and civilians ; Noted that to overcome insecurity, the security agencies can enhance intelligence gathering, improve surveillance and collaboration with local communities to anticipate and prevent attacks: "By adopting a comprehensive approach that addresses the root causes of insecurity and modernizes security capabilities and by so doing, Nigeria can effectively combat insecurity and ensure peace and stability for its citizens"

a3255.speaker: Dr Sunny Eshiotse
a3255.name: Dr Sunny Eshiotse
a3255.speech: In his paper titled "Re-imaging Nigeria's Value for Fabric for National Rebirth", called on Nigerians to value human lives rather than material things.

a3255.speaker: Dirisu Odion, NAS Capoon, Hybrid Deck, Edo-North branch
a3255.name: Dirisu Odion
a3255.title: NAS Capoon, Hybrid Deck, Edo-North branch
a3255.speech: Said the Feast of Barracuda embodies the organization's values, promoting a sense of belonging, shared purpose, and commitment to societal impact ; Said the "Barracuda" represents a fierce and powerful fish, reflecting the group's values of strength, resilience, and camaraderie, and that the "Feast of Barracuda" is a significant event in the Pyrates Confraternity and a celebration of the organisation's founding and its ideals, marked by elaborate costumes, music, and merriment: "It has become an important tradition, symbolising the bond among members and non members and their commitment to the pyrates confraternity's principles" ; Noted that the association is on the forefront of focusing on social welfare, community service, and charitable activities, that the association's ideology is to strengthen bonds among members and non members, fostering unity and solidarity, and added that the association would continue to play its role in community services, cultural heritage, social justice and good governance.

a3321.speaker: Yagana Isma’il*, 25, mother of five, Benisheik resident
a3321.name: Yagana Isma’il*
a3321.title: 25, mother of five, Benisheik resident
a3321.speech: “I will not go back to any hospital again” ; “I got pregnant with my third child just four months after my second. At some point, I felt ashamed. People mocked me for always being pregnant. I isolated myself” ; “I went to the facility four times after giving birth to my fifth daughter, but I couldn’t get the family planning method.”

a3321.speaker: Yagana Isma’il*, 25, mother of five, Benisheik resident
a3321.name: Yagana Isma’il*
a3321.title: 25, mother of five, Benisheik resident
a3321.speech: Recounted using some herbs that failed her: “I bought Gurun tazara (a herb wrapped in animal skin) from a herbalist for ₦2,500. A lot of women used to tie it on their waist for child distancing, but unfortunately, it didn’t work for me; I got pregnant 38 days after giving birth” ; “We paid him ₦4,000 for that abortion” ; “I stayed at General Hospital Damaturu for 13 days; I nearly died.”

a3321.speaker: Hamsatu Adamu, 45, Benisheik resident
a3321.name: Hamsatu Adamu
a3321.title: 45, Benisheik resident
a3321.speech: Noted how they repeatedly fight because she cannot handle the house, the children, and her husband’s expectations. “I went to the facility several times to get family planning, but I couldn’t find any method.”

a3321.speaker: Ibrahim Babagana, 29
a3321.name: Ibrahim Babagana
a3321.speech: “My wife wanted pills after our second child. She went four or five times, and each time they said it was not available. I am not happy about that. We want all methods to be accessible.”

a3321.speaker: UN Population Fund (UNFPA) 2022 report
a3321.name: UN Population Fund (UNFPA) 2022 report
a3321.speech: Estimates that nearly 121 million pregnancies worldwide each year are unintended.

a3321.speaker: Natalia Kanem, UNFPA Executive Director
a3321.name: Natalia Kanem
a3321.title: UNFPA Executive Director
a3321.speech: Said the staggering number of unintended pregnancies represents a global failure to uphold women and girls’ basic human rights.

a3321.speaker: Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey 2018
a3321.name: Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey 2018
a3321.speech: According to the survey, only about 17 per cent of married women in the country use any family planning method; the survey also puts the unmet need for family planning among married women at 19 per cent.

a3321.speaker: Baba Gana, Borno State Commissioner for Health
a3321.name: Baba Gana
a3321.title: Borno State Commissioner for Health
a3321.speech: Said in 2023 that only 6.7 per cent of married women in the state were using modern contraceptive methods.

a3321.speaker: Mala Abdulwahab, Deputy Director of the State Primary Health Care Development Agency
a3321.name: Mala Abdulwahab
a3321.title: Deputy Director of the State Primary Health Care Development Agency
a3321.speech: Said only 269 out of the 436 health facilities in the state offer family planning services.

a3321.speaker: Nigerian National Health Act 2014 (policy document)
a3321.name: Nigerian National Health Act 2014 (policy document)
a3321.speech: Affirms the right to healthcare services, including reproductive health, and shows commitment to issues around sexual and reproductive health rights.

a3321.speaker: Experts
a3321.name: Experts
a3321.speech: Say this drop in funding could reverse the progress made over the years, for a country with one of the highest maternal death rates in the world.

a3321.speaker: The United Nations
a3321.name: The United Nations
a3321.speech: Recently warned that global reductions in health aid could reverse decades of progress in tackling maternal mortality.

a3321.speaker: World Health Organisation (WHO) data
a3321.name: World Health Organisation (WHO) data
a3321.speech: Data from the WHO estimates Nigeria’s maternal mortality ratio (MMR) at 1,047 deaths per 100,000 live births, making it the country with the third-highest maternal mortality rate globally.

a3321.speaker: Aisha Modu, 27, mother of six
a3321.name: Aisha Modu
a3321.title: 27, mother of six
a3321.speech: “They kept telling me to come back when the medicines were available” ; “I bought it for ₦1,500. When I tied it around my waist, I started bleeding nonstop. My period usually lasts five days, but this one went on for 14” ; “The seller told me that if I drank it three times, I would not conceive again for three years. But that was a lie. I got pregnant six months after taking it.”

a3321.speaker: Hajara Bukar, 26, from Lawanti district, Ngamdu
a3321.name: Hajara Bukar
a3321.title: 26, from Lawanti district, Ngamdu
a3321.speech: Recounted how she too resorted to traditional methods after being turned away repeatedly at the health facility in 2020: “A friend in Maiduguri introduced me to a medicine that looked like beans. Each one was ₦1,000. I bought two, but they didn’t work. In the end, I had to buy pills from a medicine store for ₦1,700.”

a3321.speaker: World Health Organisation (WHO) report
a3321.name: World Health Organisation (WHO) report
a3321.speech: Reveals that a lack of access to comprehensive, good-quality information about sexual health increases the vulnerability of women toward diseases and other consequences, such as cancer, infertility, unsafe abortion, and maternal and infant mortality.

a3321.speaker: Abdullahi Usman, senior registrar and obstetrician at the University of Maiduguri Teaching Hospital
a3321.name: Abdullahi Usman
a3321.title: senior registrar and obstetrician at the University of Maiduguri Teaching Hospital
a3321.speech: Explained that the use of traditional herbs for abortion and contraception is a long-standing practice in rural communities; said cultural beliefs often drive such practices, though limited access to healthcare facilities and available services also contribute ; warned that the side effects of these herbs are severe: “Some commonly reported complications include gastrointestinal disturbances, liver and kidney damage, and neurological issues. In cases of abortion, it often results in incomplete abortion, where parts of the fetal tissue or placenta remain in the uterus, leading to persistent bleeding” ; added that because these methods lack standardised dosages and quality control, women face heightened risks of health complications while remaining vulnerable to unintended pregnancies.

a3321.speaker: Community Health Extension Worker (CHEW) at Benisheik Primary Health Centre maternity unit (anonymous, declined to be named)
a3321.name: Community Health Extension Worker (CHEW) at Benisheik Primary Health Centre maternity unit (anonymous
a3321.title: declined to be named)
a3321.speech: Said women are discouraged when they cannot access the specific family planning services they prefer—especially short-acting methods. “As a trusted health worker, it is embarrassing when I go around the community giving health talks, only for women to finally agree to try family planning and then discover we don’t have the commodities. It damages our credibility” ; highlighted the absence of essential medicines for post-abortion care at the facility until an intervention by the IPAS Nigeria Health Foundation in December 2024: “Drugs such as misoprostol, which is critical for managing incomplete abortions and postpartum bleeding, and ulipristal, an emergency contraceptive used in rape cases, were never available here throughout my career until IPAS supplied them. Unfortunately, the stock has already run out.”

a3321.speaker: Yagana Babagana, Facility Manager, Ngamdu Primary Health Centre
a3321.name: Yagana Babagana
a3321.title: Facility Manager, Ngamdu Primary Health Centre
a3321.speech: Described the crisis as worsening since early 2025; said there are never enough commodities, and demand is increasing daily as people become more informed; according to her, most women resist referrals to bigger hospitals: “Whenever we refer them, they refuse to go, some because they cannot afford the cost, others because they fear people will find out they are using family planning.”

a3321.speaker: Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action (1995), Section 3
a3321.name: Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action (1995)
a3321.title: Section 3
a3321.speech: Emphasises women’s right to sexual and reproductive health, including the freedom to make informed decisions without coercion, discrimination, or violence.

a3321.speaker: Nigeria’s National Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health (2018)
a3321.name: Nigeria’s National Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health (2018)
a3321.speech: Defines comprehensive care as ensuring access to information, services, and treatment—with a strong focus on women and girls.

a3321.speaker: Marka Mohammed, 32, a mother of eight
a3321.name: Marka Mohammed
a3321.title: 32, a mother of eight
a3321.speech: Admitted she wants to try family planning but is held back by fear: “I want to try the family planning methods, but I am afraid, especially of the implant and injectables, because I have heard that they may even go missing in one’s body, and I am scared not to have a child again.”

a3321.speaker: Mustapha Ibrahim, 29, a resident of Benisheik
a3321.name: Mustapha Ibrahim
a3321.title: 29, a resident of Benisheik
a3321.speech: Insisted that his wife will never use any method: “The idea of using any method is something I will not even consider. This thing can stop a woman from having a child completely. My wife will never try it.”

a3321.speaker: PREMIUM TIMES investigation (2024)
a3321.name: PREMIUM TIMES investigation (2024)
a3321.speech: Noted visible infrastructural upgrades across PHCs in Borno, but revealed that poor staffing and drug shortages were hampering service delivery, particularly in rural communities.

a3321.speaker: Mohammed Dauda, chair of the SRH Working Group at the Borno State Ministry of Health and Coordinator of Emergency Medical and Ambulatory Services
a3321.name: Mohammed Dauda
a3321.title: chair of the SRH Working Group at the Borno State Ministry of Health and Coordinator of Emergency Medical and Ambulatory Services
a3321.speech: Said that the state adopted a revised Sexual and Reproductive Health (SRH) policy in early 2025, developed with the ministry and UNFPA; according to him, Borno currently has family planning and SRH commodities in stock, overseen by two regulatory bodies: “These agencies are responsible for managing and distributing drugs at primary facilities, while BOSCHMA is partially involved with secondary facilities. Commodities are supplied based on requests from facilities” ; admitted, however, that access gaps remain: “There is sometimes a lack of accountability at the facility level, not always, but occasionally, commodities are diverted or sold. Another challenge is poor management; some facilities fail to request new supplies before stocks are exhausted” ; recommended stronger accountability frameworks and continuous training for facility managers to close these gaps.

a3321.speaker: Jalo Ahmed, Borno State Adolescent, Sexual and Reproductive Health Focal Person and Coordinator of the Community Health Influencers Promoters and Services (CHIPS) programme
a3321.name: Jalo Ahmed
a3321.title: Borno State Adolescent, Sexual and Reproductive Health Focal Person and Coordinator of the Community Health Influencers Promoters and Services (CHIPS) programme
a3321.speech: Reiterated the government’s commitment: “If there is anything like women not having access to family planning services, then maybe it is a matter of awareness. These commodities are free, but many people don’t know; others still hold negative beliefs about them” ; said the availability of family planning drugs is not a problem in Borno State: “As far as availability is concerned, we have all the drugs.”

a3342.speaker: Ifeanyi M. Nsofor, public health physician and behavioural science researcher (commentary, Project Syndicate)
a3342.name: Ifeanyi M. Nsofor
a3342.title: public health physician and behavioural science researcher (commentary, Project Syndicate)
a3342.speech: Argued that as foreign aid contracts, leaders should move towards healthy policies that boost domestic revenue, like taxing sugary drinks to curb obesity and diabetes, and that finding fiscal solutions like these, paired with the strategic use of diaspora remittances, can unlock billions in funding, steering the continent toward a healthier, self-sustained future; wrote that the current wave of aid cuts proves an uncomfortable truth, that foreign aid is inherently unreliable and can be paused, reduced, or redirected at any time; that African countries should reclaim control of their futures by adopting bold, innovative strategies to close funding gaps and build resilient, self-sufficient health systems, invest in homegrown financing solutions, and develop independent health financing mechanisms; and that "lasting independence depends on financial self-reliance."

a3342.speaker: Ifeanyi M. Nsofor, public health physician and behavioural science researcher (commentary, Project Syndicate)
a3342.name: Ifeanyi M. Nsofor
a3342.title: public health physician and behavioural science researcher (commentary, Project Syndicate)
a3342.speech: Proposed in 2019 that if African countries had allocated one percent of every remittance dollar to health insurance, the 100 billion dollars in remittances sent by the African diaspora in 2024 could have generated one billion dollars for health care, bringing the continent closer to achieving universal health coverage; added that to unlock the remittances' full potential, African governments should improve governance, strengthen accountability, and promote trust with diaspora communities.

a3342.speaker: World Health Organisation (WHO)
a3342.name: World Health Organisation (WHO)
a3342.speech: According to the WHO, up to 90pc of an individual's healthcare needs can be addressed at the primary health care (PHC) level.

a3342.speaker: WHO Sugar Tax Report
a3342.name: WHO Sugar Tax Report
a3342.speech: Shows that taxing sugary beverages reduces consumption and lowers the risk of obesity and diabetes.

a3342.speaker: Experts at the Global NCD Alliance Forum
a3342.name: Experts at the Global NCD Alliance Forum
a3342.speech: Underscored the need for stronger excise taxes across Africa to curb the growing NCD epidemic and generate sustainable revenue streams for public health investments.

a3342.speaker: 1978 Alma-Ata Declaration
a3342.name: 1978 Alma-Ata Declaration
a3342.speech: Defined primary health care as the foundation of equitable health care.

a3625.speaker: Health Ministry of the Al-Massirah Houthi rebels
a3625.name: Health Ministry of the Al-Massirah Houthi rebels
a3625.speech: Announced on Sunday that the U.S. strikes against the Houthis in Yemen killed 31 people and wounded 101.

a3625.speaker: Anis Al-Asbahi, spokesman for the Houthi Health Ministry
a3625.name: Anis Al-Asbahi
a3625.title: spokesman for the Houthi Health Ministry
a3625.speech: Wrote on the social network X that the strikes targeted the capital Sanaa, the provinces of Saada (northwest) and Al-Bayda (centre), as well as the city of Radaa (centre), noting that there were children among those killed.

a3625.speaker: Al-Massirah (Houthi rebel television station)
a3625.name: Al-Massirah (Houthi rebel television station)
a3625.speech: Announced on Saturday night that an "American-British strike" hit the Shououb area, north of the capital Sanaa, as well as Saada, a rebel stronghold in northern Yemen.

a3625.speaker: President of the United States (Donald Trump)
a3625.name: President of the United States (Donald Trump)
a3625.speech: Announced "decisive and powerful military action" against the Houthis in Yemen.

a3625.speaker: President of the United States (Donald Trump)
a3625.name: President of the United States (Donald Trump)
a3625.speech: Left a message for Iran: "Do not threaten the American people, their President (...) or the world's shipping lanes. And if you do, beware, because America will hold you fully accountable and we will not do you any favours."

a3625.speaker: The Houthis
a3625.name: The Houthis
a3625.speech: Reacted, warning that the "aggression will not go unanswered."

a3625.speaker: Political bureau of the Houthi rebels (statement broadcast by Al-Massirah, cited by Lusa)
a3625.name: Political bureau of the Houthi rebels (statement broadcast by Al-Massirah
a3625.title: cited by Lusa)
a3625.speech: "Our armed forces are ready to respond to escalation with escalation."

a3625.speaker: The Houthi rebels
a3625.name: The Houthi rebels
a3625.speech: Stressed that the decision to resume attacks on merchant shipping was taken after Israel refused to allow the delivery of humanitarian aid to the Gaza Strip, devastated by 15 months of war.

a3625.speaker: Hamas (statement)
a3625.name: Hamas (statement)
a3625.speech: Hailing "the support" given by the Houthis to the Palestinian people in the Gaza Strip, issued a statement on Saturday condemning the "American-British air aggression" and describing it as a "flagrant violation of international law."

a3729.speaker: Some of the author’s friends (supporters of Kamala Harris)
a3729.name: Some of the author’s friends (supporters of Kamala Harris)
a3729.speech: Argued that she is a woman and immigrant from a working class background; further pointed out that Black blood flows in her veins, she is not a racist and would, therefore, not pursue racist policies and programmes ; argued that Donald Trump, on the other hand, is “incompetent”, “ignorant”, “arrogant”, “egotistic”, “narcissistic”, “idiotic”, “rash”, “unpredictable”, “unconventional”, “undiplomatic”, “unapologetic”, “unrepentant”, “lunatic-like”, “dangerous” and “hyperactive right-wing racist”, who talks before he thinks, and acts before he calculates.

a3729.speaker: Karl Marx
a3729.name: Karl Marx
a3729.speech: Wrote: “The discovery of gold and silver in America, the extirpation, enslavement and entombment in the mines of the aboriginal population, the beginning of the conquest and looting of East Indies, the turning of Africa into a warren for the commercial hunting of black-skins, signalised the rosy dawn of the era of capitalist production.”

a3729.speaker: Margaret Thatcher, former Prime Minister of the United Kingdom
a3729.name: Margaret Thatcher
a3729.title: former Prime Minister of the United Kingdom
a3729.speech: Categorised the African National Congress (ANC) and its members like Nelson Mandela as “terrorists.”

a3729.speaker: Lenin
a3729.name: Lenin
a3729.speech: To use Lenin’s expression, Trump is opening the eyes of US citizens and the world “to the rottenness, mendacity and hypocrisy” of US democracy.

a3823.speaker: Muhammad Pate, Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare of Nigeria
a3823.name: Muhammad Pate
a3823.title: Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare of Nigeria
a3823.speech: Announced during the event on Thursday in Abuja that the vaccines were expected to play a pivotal role in lowering malaria-related deaths ; said the vaccine would significantly boost the country’s ongoing malaria elimination efforts: “Our target is to prioritise regions most affected by malaria, particularly in rural areas where access to healthcare is limited” ; said the vaccine rollout would begin in high-burden regions before expanding nationwide ; said global health partners, including WHO, UNICEF, and Gavi, are providing technical and financial support to ensure the successful implementation of the vaccine ; “USAID and other partners are pushing for rapid scale-up beyond the initial two states, aiming for a nationwide rollout to cover all regions of the country”.

a3823.speaker: News Agency of Nigeria (NAN)
a3823.name: News Agency of Nigeria (NAN)
a3823.speech: Reports that large clinical trials in Africa proved the vaccine, RTS,S/AS01 (Mosquirix), effective in reducing malaria cases and mortality among young children.

a4039.speaker: TSL
a4039.name: TSL
a4039.speech: "We are working through the ZMX to import commodities from other African..."

a4040.speaker: Michael Raynor, US Ambassador to Ethiopia
a4040.name: Michael Raynor
a4040.title: US Ambassador to Ethiopia
a4040.speech: "The U.S. Embassy is deeply honored by the opportunity to facilitate such a partnership, through an extraordinary initiative led by some of the world's foremost economic experts based at one of the world's foremost higher education institutions, Harvard University." ; Said that the accomplished team and proven methodologies under Haussmann's leadership have an extraordinary record throughout the world of supporting countries' efforts to identify promising areas of economic growth, to highlight constraints to such growth, and to devise strategies to address both the opportunities and the challenges.

a4040.speaker: Michael Raynor, US Ambassador to Ethiopia
a4040.name: Michael Raynor
a4040.title: US Ambassador to Ethiopia
a4040.speech: "Re-setting an economy of Ethiopia's size and complexity is far from easy work," he says, "But Ethiopia has much strength to build upon." According to the Ambassador, first and foremost it includes an exceptionally accomplished team of economic leaders and experts to drive this transformation. He said that even though the country registered positive economic and social growth recently, these gains were made at the cost of incurring significant external debt, and without commensurate progress in job-creation or private sector investment.

a4040.speaker: Government of Ethiopia
a4040.name: Government of Ethiopia
a4040.speech: Has expressed that it is working on homegrown policies to improve the economy while undertaking structural changes in its macroeconomic arena.

a4040.speaker: Yinager Dessie, Governor of the National Bank of Ethiopia (NBE)
a4040.name: Yinager Dessie
a4040.title: Governor of the National Bank of Ethiopia (NBE)
a4040.speech: Said the initiative is expected to contribute to the policy dialogue and to craft plausible professional recommendations for the new economic reform program, which the country started to implement very recently. "This economic reform focuses mainly on monetary and fiscal policy stability, structural and sectoral transformation, growth, job creation and poverty reduction," he said at the ceremony. He went on to say that even though the economy has grown for 16 years it has also seen some macroeconomic imbalance such as poor export performance and tax collection that needs to be rectified within the coming years. "We believe our economic reform agenda, which is a homegrown program, will contribute to macroeconomic stability and growth," he added. He expressed his hope that the US government initiative will support the implementation of the Ethiopian economic reform initiative, and told reporters that the initiative started when Ethiopia asked for more help to strengthen its economy.

a4123.speaker: Aaron Motsoaledi, South African Health Minister
a4123.name: Aaron Motsoaledi
a4123.title: South African Health Minister
a4123.speech: Says South Africa’s HIV/Aids programmes will not collapse despite the withdrawal of funding by the US, insisting that there are existing facilities which can absorb the affected patients; told journalists that South Africa is spending R46.8 billion on its HIV programmes, of which R7.9 billion is from Pepfar: “It is inconceivable that out of R46.8 billion spent by the country on HIV/Aids programmes, the withdrawal of R7.9 billion by President Donald Trump will immediately lead to a collapse of the entire programme” ; “We must put it categorically clear that under no circumstances will we allow this massive work, performed over a period of more than a decade and a half, to collapse and go up in smoke because President Trump has decided to do what he has done.”

a4123.speaker: Aaron Motsoaledi, South African Health Minister
a4123.name: Aaron Motsoaledi
a4123.title: South African Health Minister
a4123.speech: Acknowledged that the funding cuts had sparked stress and fear in the health sector, and among patients, but said existing funding programmes are cushioning the blow; said Pepfar supported the department of health in 27 out of 52 districts across eight provinces — understood to be “high burden” — with 2 772 public health facilities, of which only 12 were independent, specialised clinics managed by NGOs serving 63 322 clients in key populations: “When the Pepfar-funded clinics were closed … 63 322 files belonging to these key populations were moved to public health facilities” ; “It is not only Pepfar which was dealing with key populations clients but other prominent funders like the Global Fund have been supporting the country with health services for these key populations” ; said the Global Fund supports 34 designated facilities and has enabled more than 74 000 people from key populations to receive treatment.

a4123.speaker: Aaron Motsoaledi, South African Health Minister
a4123.name: Aaron Motsoaledi
a4123.title: South African Health Minister
a4123.speech: Said 8 061 out of 15 539 workers in the 27 districts funded by Pepfar had lost their jobs, and that the remainder are still employed — for now — through interim support which will last until September.

a4123.speaker: Aaron Motsoaledi, South African Health Minister
a4123.name: Aaron Motsoaledi
a4123.title: South African Health Minister
a4123.speech: Said South Africa was still on track to meet the UN’s 95-95-95 target to end HIV/Aids as a public health threat: “We know that there are 7.9 million people in South Africa who are estimated by UNAids to be HIV positive. At the moment, in terms of the UNAids target, we are at 96-79-94 and today we have 5.9 million people who are on ARV therapy” ; added that the government’s Close the Gap campaign, launched in March, aims to shift the needle from 79 to 95 by getting 1.1 million people who are HIV positive onto treatment by the end of the year, and that so far 520 700 have been started on treatment.

a4123.speaker: Researchers in the health sector
a4123.name: Researchers in the health sector
a4123.speech: Said the Trump cuts to US foreign aid could reverse the gains made in reducing the spread of the virus and the advancement of TB research.

a4265.speaker: Kartumu Yarta Boakai, First Lady of Liberia
a4265.name: Kartumu Yarta Boakai
a4265.title: First Lady of Liberia
a4265.speech: Reveals that Liberia is losing US$17.5 million annually to poor sanitation ; "The economic cost is equally staggering, with an estimated $17.5 million lost annually due to poor sanitation" ; "We can tackle this issue effectively, these funds could be redirected to development and education."

a4265.speaker: Kartumu Yarta Boakai, First Lady of Liberia
a4265.name: Kartumu Yarta Boakai
a4265.title: First Lady of Liberia
a4265.speech: Notes that open defecation, still practised by over 35% of Liberia's population, contributes to the spread of fecal-oral and water-borne diseases such as cholera, typhoid, and diarrhea - diseases, she laments, that disproportionately affect women, children, and the elderly.

a4265.speaker: Mo Ali, Managing Director of the Liberia Water and Sewer Corporation (LWSC), delivering the First Lady's speech
a4265.name: Mo Ali
a4265.title: Managing Director of the Liberia Water and Sewer Corporation (LWSC), delivering the First Lady's speech
a4265.speech: Says the day is not just about sanitation facilities; it is a moment for reflection, advocacy, and collective action on an issue that impacts millions of Liberians' dignity, health, and well-being ; "As the Champion of Maternal and Newborn Health, our First Lady has passionately advocated for the health and dignity of mothers and children. She reminds us that no mother should fear for her child's life because of a lack of safe sanitation, and no woman should face indignity or danger in accessing a basic facility. For women, particularly during pregnancy and menstruation, inadequate sanitation increases vulnerability to infections and complications that could otherwise be prevented" ; Continues that these realities are unacceptable in a world where solutions are within reach, adding that sanitation is not just a matter of infrastructure but also of justice, equality, and human dignity.

a4265.speaker: Mo Ali, Managing Director of the Liberia Water and Sewer Corporation (LWSC), delivering the First Lady's speech
a4265.name: Mo Ali
a4265.title: Managing Director of the Liberia Water and Sewer Corporation (LWSC), delivering the First Lady's speech
a4265.speech: Says the Government of Liberia is prioritizing sanitation through the ARREST Agenda, which focuses on Agriculture, Roads, Rule of Law, Education, Sanitation, and Tourism: "Sanitation is central to this framework because we understand that development cannot occur without safe water and sanitation systems" ; Says two key initiatives - the Roadmap to End Open Defecation and the Presidential WASH Compact 2030 - are cornerstones of this commitment: "These are not just policy documents; they are actionable plans that will be implemented with urgency to ensure universal sanitation access by 2030", noting that under the leadership of President Joseph Boakai and in partnership with the WASH Commission, government is taking bold steps to address the crisis head-on.

a4265.speaker: Mo Ali, Managing Director of the Liberia Water and Sewer Corporation (LWSC), delivering the First Lady's speech
a4265.name: Mo Ali
a4265.title: Managing Director of the Liberia Water and Sewer Corporation (LWSC), delivering the First Lady's speech
a4265.speech: Calls on all stakeholders - government ministries and development partners, including USAID, World Bank, UNICEF, WaterAid, and Countrywide Sanitation Activity - to intensify their efforts: "Let us promote sustainable practices, build resilient infrastructure, and ensure that sanitation solutions prioritize the needs of our women and girls" ; Suggests that education must also be at the forefront of this effort and stresses a need to raise awareness about the critical importance of sanitation, both in urban centers and in rural communities.

a4265.speaker: Mo Ali, Managing Director of the Liberia Water and Sewer Corporation (LWSC), delivering the First Lady's speech
a4265.name: Mo Ali
a4265.title: Managing Director of the Liberia Water and Sewer Corporation (LWSC), delivering the First Lady's speech
a4265.speech: Envisages a Liberia where every home, school, and community has access to clean and safe toilets, where no child dies from preventable illnesses linked to poor sanitation, and where every woman can access a toilet with dignity and security: "This is not just a dream - it is a future that we can create together" ; "To achieve this vision, we must be relentless in our actions. We must Commit resources and increase funding for sanitation infrastructure and hygiene programs", reaffirming the First Lady's and the Government of Liberia's commitments to making sanitation a priority for every Liberian.

a4425.speaker: Adama Barrow, President of the Republic of The Gambia
a4425.name: Adama Barrow
a4425.title: President of the Republic of The Gambia
a4425.speech: On multilateralism and UN reform: “It is an honour for The Gambia to participate in the 79th Session of the United Nations General Assembly”; welcomed the initiative presented by Secretary-General Guterres at the Summit of the Future under the theme “Multilateral Solutions for a Better Tomorrow” and said “My delegation firmly believes that the path to a better tomorrow lies in multilateralism and closer international cooperation”; said the international community must recommit to implementing the resolutions of the Summit of the Future to tackle climate change, poverty, transnational crimes and conflict, and that these incidents “underscore the urgent need for comprehensive reforms within the United Nations system, particularly the UN Security Council and the International Financial Institutions.”

a4425.speaker: Adama Barrow, President of the Republic of The Gambia
a4425.name: Adama Barrow
a4425.title: President of the Republic of The Gambia
a4425.speech: On development and Least Developed Countries: said the framework of the Sustainable Development Goals is central to The Gambia’s national agenda; said that like many Least Developed Countries The Gambia faces huge challenges that pose serious threats to its survival as a nation, and that “the global community needs to assist the Least Developed Countries, especially to address the burden of inequality, build more robust economies, and create policy space for economic growth”, calling for increased investment in capacity building to tackle the debt burden and for joint efforts to bridge the digital divide and support technology transfer.

a4425.speaker: Adama Barrow, President of the Republic of The Gambia
a4425.name: Adama Barrow
a4425.title: President of the Republic of The Gambia
a4425.speech: On gender and youth: said The Gambia is fully committed to the global call for gender equality and that “empowering women translates into community empowerment and, ultimately, inclusive development”; “As President, I will continue to ensure that women and girls are protected and given the necessary space to contribute meaningfully to our national development agenda”; said a recent consultative summit recommended a sharper focus on innovation and climate change, gender equity, bridging the digital divide and global governance, and that his government commits to aligning national priorities with global benchmarks and to using transformative solutions to create greater opportunities for all.

a4425.speaker: Adama Barrow, President of the Republic of The Gambia
a4425.name: Adama Barrow
a4425.title: President of the Republic of The Gambia
a4425.speech: On climate and the ICJ: said The Gambia last year co-sponsored UN General Assembly consensus resolution 77/276 seeking to engage the International Court of Justice on the obligations of States regarding climate change, submitted its written statement to the ICJ last August, and looks forward to participating in the oral hearings later this year in The Hague.

a4425.speaker: Adama Barrow, President of the Republic of The Gambia
a4425.name: Adama Barrow
a4425.title: President of the Republic of The Gambia
a4425.speech: On human rights and democracy at home: said The Gambia remains steadfast in promoting human rights and establishing a vibrant democratic environment through a National Human Rights Commission and an independent judiciary; “I am happy to report that, since 2017, The Gambia has neither recorded a single political prisoner, nor has any journalist or human rights activist been jailed”; noted The Gambia was recognised in August 2024 as one of Africa’s leading defenders of freedom of expression, ranked third in Article 19’s Global Expression Report 2024.

a4425.speaker: Adama Barrow, President of the Republic of The Gambia
a4425.name: Adama Barrow
a4425.title: President of the Republic of The Gambia
a4425.speech: On transitional justice and peacebuilding: said that with the help of the international community The Gambia is steadily taking steps to bring closure to the saga of the victims of dictatorship, has successfully managed the Transitional Justice and Reform processes, and counts on support in the next critical stages of ensuring justice, reconciliation and reparation; expressed appreciation for the support of the UN Peacebuilding Commission.

a4425.speaker: Adama Barrow, President of the Republic of The Gambia
a4425.name: Adama Barrow
a4425.title: President of the Republic of The Gambia
a4425.speech: On global conflicts and Palestine: said the ongoing conflicts in Palestine, Sudan, the Sahel, Ukraine and Russia, the DRC, Libya and other conflict zones demand the international community’s immediate intervention; called on the international community to prioritise support for the post-conflict reconstruction of Gaza and the improvement of economic conditions in the West Bank; said “The Israeli occupation, expansion of settlements, blockade of Gaza, and restrictions in the West Bank, together with the threat of intensifying the war to a regional conflict, continue to worsen the ongoing tensions in the Middle East”; called on the UN, the international community and OIC Member States to urgently bring about permanent peace in Palestine and, as Chair of the OIC, committed to stepping up diplomatic efforts toward a two-state arrangement within the recognised pre-1967 borders; said The Gambia has stood as a beacon of hope for the oppressed Rohingya Muslims of Myanmar and that his office will be available for dialogue between Iran, its neighbours and Western partners.

a4425.speaker: Adama Barrow, President of the Republic of The Gambia
a4425.name: Adama Barrow
a4425.title: President of the Republic of The Gambia
a4425.speech: On Morocco and China: commended the efforts of the Kingdom of Morocco and the viability of the Moroccan Autonomy Initiative as a platform for a UN-led dialogue on the Moroccan Sahara conflict; said that with regard to the One China Principle “we continue to stand with China”, that “The People’s Republic of China represents renewed hope for global rebalancing towards justice, peace, and development” and that China’s generous support through its development cooperation initiatives has proven usefully impactful and strategic.

a4425.speaker: Adama Barrow, President of the Republic of The Gambia
a4425.name: Adama Barrow
a4425.title: President of the Republic of The Gambia
a4425.speech: On migration, sanctions and development assistance: said migration significantly contributes to the growth of both home and host countries and that the international community should address migration in a regulated manner and decriminalise it; said The Gambia is collaborating with relevant countries to improve the plight of migrants and is duty-bound to respect migrants’ rights; said dictatorship, conflict, climate change, poverty and lack of opportunities are root causes of migration and that economic sanctions also contribute to forced migration, citing “The long-standing U.S. embargo against Cuba” as an example which “should give way to renewed good neighbourliness and cooperative relations between the two nations”; said “The international community should address inequality with compassion and fulfil the commitment to the official development assistance pledge made by donor countries.”

a4425.speaker: Adama Barrow, President of the Republic of The Gambia
a4425.name: Adama Barrow
a4425.title: President of the Republic of The Gambia
a4425.speech: In conclusion: said the international community must prioritise diplomacy, dialogue and mutual understanding, urged the private sector to collaborate with governments, and said “Let us embrace a message of hope, resilience, and optimism for the future. Together, we can create a world where peace, sustainable development, and human dignity are not mere dreams but a reality for all.”

a4445.speaker: African Sun (hotel group)
a4445.name: African Sun (hotel group)
a4445.speech: Anticipates strong recovery in the second quarter (Q2) supported by the domestic market and conference business after key performance indicators plunged during the first three months to March 31, 2025.

a4683.speaker: Vladimir Putin, President of Russia
a4683.name: Vladimir Putin
a4683.title: President of Russia
a4683.speech: Welcomed the increase in the volume of trade between Moscow and Ouagadougou, expressing the wish that “this trend be maintained”, and added: “We must work together to further strengthen economic ties and diversify mutual trade”, while stressing the importance of humanitarian aid for Burkina Faso.

a4683.speaker: Vladimir Putin, President of Russia
a4683.name: Vladimir Putin
a4683.title: President of Russia
a4683.speech: On security, assured that his country would continue to support Burkina Faso in its fight against radical groups: “We will continue to help the Republic restore law and constitutional order, and to provide assistance in suppressing the radical groups that remain in certain regions of Burkina Faso.”

a4683.speaker: Captain Ibrahim Traoré, Head of State of Burkina Faso
a4683.name: Captain Ibrahim Traoré
a4683.title: Head of State of Burkina Faso
a4683.speech: Speaking in Russian, argued for a “transfer of knowledge” rather than mere aid, stating that his country wishes to broaden cooperation with Russia beyond the defence and security sectors to include education, science and machinery; expressed his desire to see Russian universities established in Burkina Faso, to make the country a knowledge hub for young Africans.

a4683.speaker: Captain Ibrahim Traoré, Head of State of Burkina Faso
a4683.name: Captain Ibrahim Traoré
a4683.title: Head of State of Burkina Faso
a4683.speech: Also recalled that “the war in Burkina today is not only terrorism”, describing it as a “war against the imperialism that wants to seize our lands.”

a4737.speaker: U.S. Strategy Toward Sub-Saharan Africa (August 2022 document)
a4737.name: U.S. Strategy Toward Sub-Saharan Africa (August 2022 document)
a4737.speech: Promised to develop an African continent that “lives in liberty, peace, and growing prosperity,” and promised “security dividends” that the continent has reaped few tangible results from.

a4737.speaker: Gibson Nyikadzino, Zimbabwean journalist and international relations analyst
a4737.name: Gibson Nyikadzino
a4737.title: Zimbabwean journalist and international relations analyst
a4737.speech: “The most unfortunate development geopolitically is that the relationship between Africa and the United States or any other Western country has never changed over the past 20 years” ; “It is only based on exploitation, so there is a continuity of an unequal relationship.”

a4737.speaker: David Vine, former American University Professor
a4737.name: David Vine
a4737.title: former American University Professor
a4737.speech: Estimated that the U.S. army had maintained a presence in at least 26 African countries by 2021, with Niger, Djibouti and Somalia serving as key hosts for large military facilities on the continent.

a4737.speaker: Eniola Anuoluwapo Soyemi, Oxford University Senior Research Fellow
a4737.name: Eniola Anuoluwapo Soyemi
a4737.title: Oxford University Senior Research Fellow
a4737.speech: Calculated that in Somalia alone more than 2.5 billion dollars were pumped into counterterrorism assistance between 2007 and 2020.

a4737.speaker: 2020 U.S. Lead Inspector General’s audit
a4737.name: 2020 U.S. Lead Inspector General’s audit
a4737.speech: Suggested that the United States failed to rein in the terrorist threat in Somalia, with al-Shabab remaining “adaptive, resilient and capable of attacking.”

a4737.speaker: Elizabeth Shackelford, former U.S. career diplomat
a4737.name: Elizabeth Shackelford
a4737.title: former U.S. career diplomat
a4737.speech: Observed that as U.S. security assistance soared from 200,000 dollars per year to 18 million dollars in 2018, a sudden influx of training, weapons and intelligence led local powers to “see military solutions to any problem,” which resulted in Burkina Faso’s fall into one of the world’s worst-impacted regions by terrorism.

a4737.speaker: Adhere Cavince, Kenyan scholar on international relations
a4737.name: Adhere Cavince
a4737.title: Kenyan scholar on international relations
a4737.speech: “The huge resources dedicated to counterterrorism have been taken away from the enterprise of economic development, leaving many countries where the United States operates in dire need of development” ; “Instead of focusing on investing in productive sectors that would get Africa’s youth away from terrorism, the United States is inadvertently fueling the vice that it aims to eradicate” ; pointed out that young people who lack access to jobs often fall prey to recruitment by terrorist groups ; “Similarly, the U.S. penchant for propagating regime change in Africa has created volatility that has only fueled the emergence of militant groups. This has resulted in ungovernable spaces in countries like Libya and Somalia, giving room for extremists and terrorist outfits to thrive” ; “The U.S. approach to security is creating turmoil in Africa. It is cutting economic activity and driving governance by guns.”

a4737.speaker: Adhere Cavince, Kenyan scholar on international relations
a4737.name: Adhere Cavince
a4737.title: Kenyan scholar on international relations
a4737.speech: Said there are not enough international terrorist groups in Africa to pose a direct security threat to Washington, which makes “the overwhelming U.S. groud-based forces numbering over 6,500 and dozens of military bases therefore not warranted.”

a4737.speaker: Global Terrorism Index report (latest)
a4737.name: Global Terrorism Index report (latest)
a4737.speech: Flagged a dramatic increase in terrorism-related deaths and a 1,266 percent jump in incidents in the Sahel from 2007 to 2023.

a4737.speaker: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees
a4737.name: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees
a4737.speech: According to it, some 12.5 million people remain in need of humanitarian assistance in the Lake Chad Basin region, with 5.3 million people suffering food insecurity.

a4737.speaker: The Intercept (U.S. news outlet reports)
a4737.name: The Intercept (U.S. news outlet reports)
a4737.speech: Reported that U.S. forces launched about 300 drone strikes and commando raids in Somalia without apologizing to the families of the civilians killed.

a4737.speaker: Emmanuel Yenshu Vubo, professor of sociology at Cameroon’s University of Buea
a4737.name: Emmanuel Yenshu Vubo
a4737.title: professor of sociology at Cameroon’s University of Buea
a4737.speech: “Since 2020, Africa has seen more political unrest, violent extremism, and democratic reversals than any other region in the world” ; “U.S. engagement with Africa has long been de-prioritized, with successive administrations devoting negligible attention and resources to resolving conflicts and countering terrorism.”

a4737.speaker: Protesters across the African continent
a4737.name: Protesters across the African continent
a4737.speech: Flooded the streets chanting “U.S. Army: You leave, you move, you vanish.”

a4737.speaker: Adhere Cavince, Kenyan scholar on international relations
a4737.name: Adhere Cavince
a4737.title: Kenyan scholar on international relations
a4737.speech: “Behind increasing disaffection of African countries is the view that America is perpetuating hegemonic relations with Africa, the kind that reeks of neocolonial tendencies, where the United States is all-powerful with military bases all around yet cannot work jointly with hosting governments to deliver sustainable development and security to the local population” ; explained that Africa is yearning for transformative initiatives to boost investment, trade, infrastructure and technology development, noting that many countries regard their partnership with Washington as “lost decades in terms of development.”

a4737.speaker: Adhere Cavince, Kenyan scholar on international relations
a4737.name: Adhere Cavince
a4737.title: Kenyan scholar on international relations
a4737.speech: Held a cautious view of Biden’s “rushed attempt to fulfill a promise to visit Africa made over two years ago”: “Angola is only a platform for him to project U.S. global economic visibility, rather than a desire to drive inclusive development in a manner that can safeguard the security and safety of ordinary people” ; warned that “Africa is the youngest continent by population and is home to huge deposits of natural resources. Any partner that ignores Africa risks its own future,” calling on Washington to ditch a zero-sum mindset and engage Africa constructively.

a4791.speaker: African Development Bank (AfDB) 2025 Country Focus Report
a4791.name: African Development Bank (AfDB) 2025 Country Focus Report
a4791.speech: Has cautioned that Eswatini's fiscal position is highly vulnerable due to its heavy reliance on SACU receipts; explains that through SACU's revenue-sharing formula, any slowdown in regional trade volumes can shrink the customs pool and reduce Eswatini's allocation; highlights that reduced Chinese exports to South Africa and neighbouring states, together with wider US-China tariff disputes, pose a risk to the stability of Eswatini's fiscal accounts; reports that falling oil prices, while easing inflationary pressure, also suppress customs collections, further narrowing fiscal space.

a4791.speaker: Neal Rijkenberg, Minister for Finance of Eswatini
a4791.name: Neal Rijkenberg
a4791.title: Minister for Finance of Eswatini
a4791.speech: Said the country had been warned since time immemorial about the over reliance on SACU. "The new risk is that new tariffs result in lower growth, but are not indicating recessions. So the risk is that SACU does not grow, not that it gets reduced."

a4791.speaker: African Development Bank (AfDB) 2025 Country Focus Report
a4791.name: African Development Bank (AfDB) 2025 Country Focus Report
a4791.speech: Projects that Eswatini's GDP will rebound to 6.5 per cent in 2025, driven by dam construction, new mining activity and energy investments, but emphasises that this outlook is fragile; states that the fiscal deficit, which narrowed to 0.1 per cent of GDP in 2024, could widen again if SACU transfers decline.

a4791.speaker: African Development Bank (AfDB) 2025 Country Focus Report
a4791.name: African Development Bank (AfDB) 2025 Country Focus Report
a4791.speech: Notes that official development assistance remains a key support pillar, with 94 per cent of aid coming from the United States: "Any reductions in US support would directly affect critical programmes, including HIV treatment for over 230 000 people and funding for women's enterprises."

a4791.speaker: African Development Bank (AfDB) 2025 Country Focus Report
a4791.name: African Development Bank (AfDB) 2025 Country Focus Report
a4791.speech: Has raised concerns over governance weaknesses and social challenges, saying these challenges continue to hinder Eswatini's ability to mobilise capital for long-term development; reports that governance indicators have declined in recent years, with Eswatini falling from 85th place in 2017 to 130th in 2023 on Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index and slipping on the Ibrahim Index of African Governance; observes that weak institutions, opaque procurement systems and delays in implementing the Fiscal Adjustment Plan have raised fears with policymaking perceived as benefitting a narrow group rather than the broader population.

a4791.speaker: African Development Bank (AfDB) 2025 Country Focus Report
a4791.name: African Development Bank (AfDB) 2025 Country Focus Report
a4791.speech: Calculates that tax revenue stood at 29.4 per cent of GDP in 2024, well below the 13.2 per cent annual growth required to meet development goals by 2030, and that with nearly 62 per cent of the workforce employed in the informal sector, broadening the tax base remains a significant challenge; states that State-owned enterprises continue to drain the fiscus, receiving transfers equivalent to 3.5 per cent of GDP while contributing little in return; highlights that unemployment is estimated at 37.6 per cent, with youth unemployment at an alarming 65 per cent, that more than half of Eswatini's population lives in poverty and that inequality remains entrenched with a Gini index of 54.6.

a4853.speaker: Experts (many), on the foreign aid freeze
a4853.name: Experts (many)
a4853.title: on the foreign aid freeze
a4853.speech: Many experts warn that diseases will surge as a result of U.S. President Trump's spending freeze on foreign aid.

a4853.speaker: Aaron Motsoaledi, Health Minister of South Africa, and Bjorn Lomborg, President of the Copenhagen Consensus
a4853.name: Aaron Motsoaledi
a4853.title: Health Minister of South Africa, and Bjorn Lomborg, President of the Copenhagen Consensus
a4853.speech: Expressed their dismay and concern over the dismantling of the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), which distributes tens of billions of dollars' worth of overseas aid every year.

a4853.speaker: Aaron Motsoaledi, Health Minister of South Africa, and Bjorn Lomborg, President of the Copenhagen Consensus
a4853.name: Aaron Motsoaledi
a4853.title: Health Minister of South Africa, and Bjorn Lomborg, President of the Copenhagen Consensus
a4853.speech: Argue that international aid organizations should commit a lot more money and energy towards the fight against TB, particularly in the context of Trump's spending freeze on foreign aid which will likely result in a surge of diseases such as TB ; "We know how to defeat the disease. It would take surprisingly few resources. Research for the Copenhagen Consensus think-tank shows that additional expenditure of $6.2 billion annually could save about a million lives a year over coming decades, making this one of the very best possible development policies."

a4853.speaker: Aaron Motsoaledi, Health Minister of South Africa, and Bjorn Lomborg, President of the Copenhagen Consensus
a4853.name: Aaron Motsoaledi
a4853.title: Health Minister of South Africa, and Bjorn Lomborg, President of the Copenhagen Consensus
a4853.speech: Argued that during this time of uncertainty about the future role of the world's biggest donor, the Global Fund stands as a beacon of hope: "Since the beginning of the millennium, the Geneva-based multilateral organization has been fighting one of humanity's oldest scourges, infectious disease—and specifically the three big killers, malaria, HIV, and tuberculosis... Now, the time is ripe to sharpen its focus on tuberculosis" ; noted that nearly one-third of the Global Fund's 2023-2025 allocations, some $4.17 billion, went to malaria and $6.48 billion to HIV, while tuberculosis prevention and control has been allocated $2.4 billion or just 18% of allocations, even though tuberculosis now kills more people than HIV and malaria together ; "Tuberculosis has become an illness of poverty... Tuberculosis has gone from risking the lives of all to just killing those that nobody cares enough about" ; "The Global Fund is in the middle of its three-year replenishment cycle... The world needs to be generous because the Global Fund has shown that it is one of the very best ways to achieve good in the world. And the Global Fund – as well as development agencies everywhere – need to focus more on the illness that is claiming the most lives, and where investment can deliver an astonishing return on investment."

a4853.speaker: Trump administration / US government
a4853.name: Trump administration / US government
a4853.speech: Announced huge cuts to USAID's workforce and the immediate suspension of almost all of its aid programmes, and a 90-day freeze on funding for aid projects while it undertakes a "review" to ensure they align with President Trump's priorities ; targeted USAID in particular, saying the agency's spending is totally unexplainable, and singled out certain projects as examples of how the agency is, in its view, wasting taxpayers' money.

a4853.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a4853.name: Donald Trump
a4853.title: US President
a4853.speech: A long-term critic of overseas spending, has said it needs to be brought into line with his "America First" strategy.

a4853.speaker: Bjorn Lomborg, President of the Copenhagen Consensus (exclusive interview with Daily Independent)
a4853.name: Bjorn Lomborg
a4853.title: President of the Copenhagen Consensus (exclusive interview with Daily Independent)
a4853.speech: "There is hope that African leaders with adhere to recent global modeling exercise conducted for the Global Plan to End TB, 2023–2030. The Global Plan provides aspirational scenarios to reduce the number of TB deaths and the TB incidence by 90% and 80%, respectively, by 2030 relative to 2015 in line with the UN's Sustainable Development Goals. The Global Plan, commissioned by the Stop TB partnership, is a collaborative and inclusive document, developed with the input of numerous partners, including the Copenhagen Consensus, stakeholders, and experts over the course of almost 2 years. The plan calls for scaling up existing tools for addressing TB— such as molecular diagnostics and approaches for early case finding— as well as funding and deploying innovations, such as digital adherence tools and a new vaccine over the period 2023 to 2030."

a4853.speaker: Global Plan to End TB, 2023–2030 (report commissioned by the Stop TB Partnership)
a4853.name: Global Plan to End TB
a4853.title: 2023–2030 (report commissioned by the Stop TB Partnership)
a4853.speech: Reports that US$ 250 billion in funding would be required between 2023 and 2030 to implement the plan, leading to 6.6 million averted deaths and 234 million averted disability-adjusted-life-years; in 2030, incremental costs total US$ 5.2 billion, and in 2050, an extra US$ 2.6 billion is required; with this funding, incremental averted cases and deaths are 370,000 and 85,000, respectively, in the first year and continue rising over time.

a4969.speaker: US Department of Homeland Security
a4969.name: US Department of Homeland Security
a4969.speech: Justified the decision by saying their home countries refused 'to take them back.'

a4969.speaker: US Supreme Court (June ruling, majority opinion)
a4969.name: US Supreme Court (June ruling
a4969.title: majority opinion)
a4969.speech: Ruled that migrants may be sent to third countries without notice or legal recourse, overruling protections in the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment that prevent deportations to countries where people are at risk of torture; the conservative majority set aside those safeguards, granting the government broad authority to expedite deportations, and the majority opinion provided no reasons for its findings.

a4969.speaker: US Supreme Court (minority opinion)
a4969.name: US Supreme Court (minority opinion)
a4969.speech: Stressed that life-and-death matters required careful attention and adherence to the rule of law.

a4969.speaker: 2023 US State Department report
a4969.name: 2023 US State Department report
a4969.speech: Detailed Rwanda's harsh and life-threatening prison conditions.

a4969.speaker: US State Department report (on Eswatini)
a4969.name: US State Department report (on Eswatini)
a4969.speech: Documented human rights abuses there, including extrajudicial killings and torture.

a4969.speaker: The New York Times
a4969.name: The New York Times
a4969.speech: Recently reported that a US diplomat urged Eswatini officials in March to accept deportees even though another State Department report documented human rights abuses there.

a4969.speaker: The New York Times
a4969.name: The New York Times
a4969.speech: In June revealed the Trump administration pressured 58 countries, many in Africa, to accept deportees, an 'intense diplomatic campaign' that targeted nations facing US travel bans, visa restrictions or tariffs.

a4969.speaker: Southern Africa Litigation Centre
a4969.name: Southern Africa Litigation Centre
a4969.speech: On 31 July filed an urgent High Court application against Eswatini's correctional services department for denying the deportees access to legal counsel.

a4969.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State
a4969.name: Marco Rubio
a4969.title: US Secretary of State
a4969.speech: During an April cabinet meeting emphasised that instead of asking 'what is good for the world,' every diplomatic decision would now ask: 'Is it good for America?' He said that US foreign policy would be guided by whether it made America stronger, safer, or richer.

a4969.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State
a4969.name: Marco Rubio
a4969.title: US Secretary of State
a4969.speech: Said the Trump administration was 'actively searching for other countries to take people from third countries,' stressing this was a global effort: 'We're approaching nations to ask, "Will you take some of the most despicable human beings as a favour to us? The farther from America, the better."'

a4969.speaker: CBS News
a4969.name: CBS News
a4969.speech: In May reported the US had asked Angola, Benin, Equatorial Guinea and Libya to accept deportees.

a4969.speaker: Yusuf Tuggar, Nigeria's Foreign Minister
a4969.name: Yusuf Tuggar
a4969.title: Nigeria's Foreign Minister
a4969.speech: According to him, the US was 'mounting considerable pressure' on African countries to accept deportees; he said Nigeria outright rejected the deal, saying the country had enough problems of its own.

a4969.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a4969.name: Donald Trump
a4969.title: US President
a4969.speech: Pledged to 'make America great again,' which has translated into a sharp focus on expelling foreign nationals convicted of violent crimes, prioritising US interests above all else; in his first six months in office he dismantled US soft power by cutting foreign aid, insisting America had gotten a raw deal from its global counterparts.

a4969.speaker: Dr Kelly E Stone, Senior Consultant, Justice and Violence Prevention, Institute for Security Studies (ISS) Pretoria
a4969.name: Dr Kelly E Stone
a4969.title: Senior Consultant, Justice and Violence Prevention, Institute for Security Studies (ISS) Pretoria
a4969.speech: Argues the US's approach reflects a troubling perception of Africa as a 'dumping ground' for foreign nationals convicted of violent crimes, rather than a strategic partner in global security, and that such policies will likely erode years of diplomatic progress and US-Africa relations, especially in intelligence, counter-terrorism and anti-trafficking; writes that these actions show Trump is using diplomacy to secure America's short-term interests at the expense of human rights and regional security in Africa, and that the deportation policies 'serve the interests of no one, including America.'

a5052.speaker: Waleed Al-Bahar, acting director general of the Kuwait Fund for Arab Economic Development (KFAED)
a5052.name: Waleed Al-Bahar
a5052.title: acting director general of the Kuwait Fund for Arab Economic Development (KFAED)
a5052.speech: Said the agreements reflect Kuwait's commitment to international cooperation in development, peacebuilding and humanitarian assistance ; “This renewed partnership with the UK brings together experience and shared purpose to support the most vulnerable communities in Sudan and Somalia.” “It also underscores Kuwait's leading role in humanitarian diplomacy both regionally and globally.”

a5052.speaker: Mamadou Sow, head of the ICRC Regional Delegation for Gulf Cooperation Council countries
a5052.name: Mamadou Sow
a5052.title: head of the ICRC Regional Delegation for Gulf Cooperation Council countries
a5052.speech: Praised the cooperation as a sign of united humanitarian resolve ; “This support extends beyond financial aid—it sends a clear message of solidarity with the Somali people.” “It aims to restore vital services in long-marginalized communities that have endured decades of hardship.”

a5065.speaker: Eyobel Gebresenbet, director of reverse engineering at the Ethiopian Biotechnology Institute
a5065.name: Eyobel Gebresenbet
a5065.title: director of reverse engineering at the Ethiopian Biotechnology Institute
a5065.speech: Said the thresher aims to improve quality of life, strengthen value chains, and contribute to food security ; "It will also save the crop from unseasonal rain and create job opportunities for the manufacturers and youths from rural areas who migrate to urban areas," he told Fortune ; said it is too expensive to buy the engine.

a5065.speaker: Eyobel Gebresenbet, director of reverse engineering at the Ethiopian Biotechnology Institute
a5065.name: Eyobel Gebresenbet
a5065.title: director of reverse engineering at the Ethiopian Biotechnology Institute
a5065.speech: Said the Institute plans to pilot the machine in Zeway.

a5065.speaker: Bogale Tekle, vice-dean of Wolqite Polytechnic College
a5065.name: Bogale Tekle
a5065.title: vice-dean of Wolqite Polytechnic College
a5065.speech: Said Wolkite Polytechnic College was selected for the project because of its human resources, machinery and convenient workshops ; "It produces cleaner agricultural products," he said. "It also reduces the amount of hard labour and drudgery."

a5065.speaker: Ministry of Agriculture (data)
a5065.name: Ministry of Agriculture (data)
a5065.speech: During the harvest season, 25 to 30pc of the produced crops are wasted, according to data from the Ministry of Agriculture.

a5065.speaker: Daniel Dentamo, communications team leader at the Ministry of Agriculture
a5065.name: Daniel Dentamo
a5065.title: communications team leader at the Ministry of Agriculture
a5065.speech: Said that since the machine would be expensive, farmers should consider organising themselves to buy the machine ; "If the farmers can buy the machine easily, it will save energy and time."

a5065.speaker: Habtamu Tsegaye, crop value chain advisor at USAID's Feed the Future Ethiopia programme
a5065.name: Habtamu Tsegaye
a5065.title: crop value chain advisor at USAID's Feed the Future Ethiopia programme
a5065.speech: Says that the private sector should take the lead in distributing these machines to the farmers ; "It is very difficult for the manufacturers to both produce the machine and distribute it to the farmer" ; says that the government should support and work to link the manufacturer and farmer in order to make the process transparent.

a5065.speaker: Fentahun Tesfa, assistant professor at Bahir Dar University's College of Agriculture & Environmental Sciences
a5065.name: Fentahun Tesfa
a5065.title: assistant professor at Bahir Dar University's College of Agriculture & Environmental Sciences
